modules.name: std::char
modules.doc:
# Char Module  
  
Character and UTF-8 scalar classification helpers.  
  
`char` is a native Unicode scalar. Byte-backed text traversal keeps offsets  
internal to string and cursor helpers, while the classification helpers in  
this module accept native `char` values directly. This keeps scalar semantics  
ergonomic while keeping ASCII-only behavior explicit:  
  
- `isAscii*` helpers classify `char` values without byte casts.  
- `isAlpha`, `isNumeric`, `isAlphanumeric`, and `isWhitespace` classify  
  Unicode scalar `char` values.  
  
## Examples  
  
```ignis  
import Char from "std::char";  
  
let letter: char = 'é';  
let digit: char = '５';  
  
letter.isAlpha();        // true  
digit.isNumeric();       // true  
Char::isAsciiAlpha('A'); // true  
```

modules.name: std::cli
modules.doc:
# CLI Module  
  
Bounded clap-like command-line parsing helpers.  
  
## Purpose  
  
This module provides a small, reviewable command builder and argv parser for  
common Ignis CLI entrypoints.  
  
It is inspired by clap-style APIs, but it is intentionally narrower:  
callers declare a command, register supported flags/options, and then parse a  
`Vector<String>` or the current process arguments into owned `Matches`.  
  
## Supported grammar  
  
| Form | Supported | Notes |  
|------|-----------|-------|  
| `--flag` | Yes | Declared boolean flag |  
| `-f` | Yes | Declared short flag |  
| `--output file` | Yes | Declared valued option consumes next argv item |  
| `-o file` | Yes | Declared short valued option consumes next argv item |  
| positional args | Yes | Preserved in order |  
| `--` terminator | Yes | All later tokens become positionals |  
| `--opt=value` | No | Intentionally out of scope |  
| grouped short flags (`-abc`) | No | Intentionally out of scope |  
| defaults / env injection | No | Intentionally out of scope |  
| subcommands | No | Intentionally out of scope |  
  
## Parsing lifecycle  
  
```text  
  Command spec  
  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────┐  
  │ new(name)                                 │  
  │ aboutText(...)                            │  
  │ flag(...) / option(...)                   │  
  └────────────────────┬──────────────────────┘  
                       │  
                       ▼  
  argv scan  
  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────┐  
  │ parse(&args) or parseProcess()            │  
  │ - detect `--`                             │  
  │ - match long/short specs                  │  
  │ - collect owned option values             │  
  │ - preserve ordered positionals            │  
  └────────────────────┬──────────────────────┘  
                       │  
                       ▼  
  Result  
  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────┐  
  │ Result::OK(Matches)                       │  
  │ Result::ERROR(CliError)                   │  
  └───────────────────────────────────────────┘  
```  
  
## Ownership model  
  
- `parseProcess()` copies host argv into owned `String` values via  
  `Process::args()`.  
- `parse(&args)` clones only the values it needs to store in `Matches`.  
- `Matches::value()` and `Matches::positional()` return owned `String`  
  clones so callers do not borrow from internal parser storage.  
  
## Error model  
  
Parsing failures are explicit `Result::ERROR(CliError)` values.  
The current bounded error surface is:  
- unknown option  
- missing value for a declared valued option  
  
## Help rendering  
  
`renderHelp()` is deterministic:  
- usage line first  
- about text next when present  
- option listing in declaration order  
  
## Example  
  
```ignis  
import Cli from "std::cli";  
  
function main(): i32 {  
  let mut command: Cli::Command = Cli::Command::new("tool");  
  command.aboutText("Build project artifacts.");  
  command.flag("verbose", "v", "Enable verbose output.");  
  command.option("output", "o", "Write output file.");  
  
  match (command.parseProcess()) {  
    Result::OK(matches) -> {  
      if (matches.has("verbose")) {  
        // verbose branch  
      }  
      return 0;  
    },  
    Result::ERROR(error) -> {  
      // print error.message or renderHelp()  
      return 1;  
    },  
  };  
}  
```

modules.name: std::collections
modules.doc:
# Collections  
  
Hash-based collection entrypoint.  
  
## Overview  
  
`std::collections` re-exports deterministic hash-table containers and the  
`Hash`/`Eq` traits needed by user-defined keys.  
  
## Exports  
  
| Export     | Description                                      |  
|------------|--------------------------------------------------|  
| `HashMap`  | Open-addressed key/value map with linear probing |  
| `HashSet`  | Set built on top of `HashMap`                    |  
| `BitSet`   | Dense deterministic membership set for `u32` ids |  
| `Hash`     | Trait for feeding key bytes into `Hasher`        |  
| `Eq`       | Marker for canonical equality support            |  
  
## Notes  
  
Hashing is deterministic, not randomized. Do not expose these collections as  
a denial-of-service boundary for attacker-controlled keys without additional  
protections.

modules.name: std::collections::hash_map
modules.doc:
# HashMap  
  
Deterministic open-addressed hash map with linear probing.  
  
## Overview  
  
`HashMap<K, V>` stores keys and values in parallel contiguous buffers.  
Lookup uses:  
  
- deterministic hashing via `std::hash::Hasher`  
- open addressing  
- linear probing  
- tombstones for removed entries  
  
The map grows when the configured load factor would be exceeded.  
Capacity is always managed in buckets, not bytes.  
  
## Key Requirements  
  
Keys must satisfy `Hash & Eq`.  
  
In practice that means user-defined key types usually provide:  
  
- `@implements(Hash, Eq)` on the record  
- a `hash(&self, hasher: &mut Hasher): void` method  
- an `equals(&self, other: &K): boolean` method  
  
## Bucket States  
  
```text  
  state = 0  -> empty  
  state = 1  -> occupied  
  state = 2  -> tombstone  
```  
  
Empty buckets stop probing. Tombstones preserve probe chains after remove.  
  
## Memory Layout  
  
```text  
  HashMap<K, V>  
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  
  │ states:  [E|O|T|O|...]                                    │  
  │ hashes:  [0|h|0|h|...]                                    │  
  │ keys:    [ |K| |K|...]                                    │  
  │ values:  [ |V| |V|...]                                    │  
  │ length: active occupied buckets                           │  
  │ tombstones: removed buckets still participating in probe  │  
  │ capacity: total bucket count                              │  
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  
```  
  
`keys` and `values` are manual-storage buffers. Only buckets marked as  
occupied contain initialized logical elements.  
  
## Probe Sequence  
  
A lookup starts at `hash % capacity` and advances one slot at a time until:  
  
- it finds an empty bucket (`not present`)  
- it finds a matching occupied bucket (`present`)  
- it has examined every bucket (`full-table miss`)  
  
```text  
  capacity = 8  
  start = hash % 8 = 3  
  
  index:   0   1   2   3   4   5   6   7  
  state:   E   T   O   O   T   O   E   E  
                       ^  
                       start  
  
  probe order: 3 -> 4 -> 5 -> 6  
  
  - slot 3: occupied, different key  
  - slot 4: tombstone, continue  
  - slot 5: occupied, different key  
  - slot 6: empty, stop -> key does not exist  
```  
  
## Insert / Replace Rules  
  
Insert first reserves enough capacity, then probes exactly like lookup.  
  
During probing it tracks:  
  
- the first tombstone encountered  
- whether an existing matching key was found  
  
That gives three possible outcomes:  
  
1. matching key found -> replace value  
2. no key found, tombstone seen -> reuse first tombstone  
3. no key found, no tombstone seen -> use first empty bucket  
  
## Drop Behavior  
  
`HashMap` owns both the key and the value stored in an occupied bucket.  
  
That means:  
  
- replacing an entry drops the previous key and returns the previous value  
- removing an entry drops the key and returns the value  
- `clear()` drops every occupied key/value pair  
- `drop()` calls `clear()` and then frees the backing buffers  
  
Tombstones do not hold logical values anymore; they only preserve probing  
structure until the next rehash.  
  
## Complexity  
  
Average-case complexity:  
  
- `insert`  -> `O(1)`  
- `get`     -> `O(1)`  
- `remove`  -> `O(1)`  
- `reserve` -> `O(n)` when rehashing occurs  
  
Worst-case probe chains are linear in the bucket count.  
  
## Example  
  
```ignis  
import Eq from "std::collections";  
import Hash from "std::collections";  
import HashMap from "std::collections";  
import Hasher from "std::hash";  
  
@implements(Hash, Eq)  
record Key {  
  id: i32;  
  
  hash(&self, hasher: &mut Hasher): void {  
    let mut state: &mut Hasher = hasher;  
    state.writeI32(self.id);  
  }  
  
  equals(&self, other: &Key): boolean {  
    return self.id == other.id;  
  }  
}  
  
function main(): i32 {  
  let mut map: HashMap<Key, i32> = HashMap::new<Key, i32>();  
  map.insert(Key { id: 1 }, 10);  
  map.insert(Key { id: 2 }, 20);  
  
  let lookup: Key = Key { id: 2 };  
  let value: i32 = match (map.get(&lookup)) {  
    Option::SOME(found) -> *found,  
    Option::NONE -> -1,  
  };  
  
  return value;  
}  
```

Compile-time-only std placeholders for directive execution.  
  
This module remains source-only: it exists for analyzer-facing directive APIs  
and must never introduce runtime headers, objects, or link requirements.  
Only diagnostic host calls execute today. Builder and reflection handles are  
still exposed as opaque compile-time types so directive signatures can evolve  
against stable names while unsupported operations fail explicitly.

modules.name: std::compile::types
modules.doc:
Compile-time-only directive type surface.  
  
These declarations are intentionally opaque placeholders. They let directive  
signatures refer to stable `std::compile` names without exposing runtime ABI  
or pretending unsupported builder operations already work.

modules.name: std::env
modules.doc:
# Environment  
  
Safe, owned access to process environment variables on supported POSIX hosts.  
  
## Overview  
  
The `Env` namespace wraps process environment access through `std::libc`  
and returns owned `String` values instead of borrowed C pointers. This keeps  
callers insulated from host-owned environment storage.  
  
The environment is a mutable key/value map attached to the current process.  
Reads observe the current process state, and writes affect later reads in the  
same process plus child processes created after the mutation. Existing parent  
processes and already-running child processes are not modified.  
  
```text  
  Host process environment  
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  
  │ name -> NUL-terminated byte string                         │  
  │ name -> NUL-terminated byte string                         │  
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  
            │ getenv/setenv/unsetenv  
            ▼  
  Env namespace  
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  
  │ get/var copy host values into owned String results          │  
  │ set/unset mutate only the current process environment       │  
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  
```  
  
## APIs  
  
| Function      | Description                                      |  
|---------------|--------------------------------------------------|  
| `Env::get`    | Optional owned value for an environment name     |  
| `Env::has`    | Presence check without copying the value         |  
| `Env::set`    | Set or replace a value in the current process    |  
| `Env::unset`  | Remove a value from the current process          |  
| `Env::var`    | `Result` wrapper that reports missing variables  |  
| `Env::currentDir` | Current working directory as a `PathBuf`      |  
  
## Empty Values vs Missing Values  
  
`Env::get("NAME")` returns `Option::SOME(String::create(""))` when `NAME`  
exists and is set to the empty string. It returns `Option::NONE` only when the  
variable is absent. Use `Env::has` when presence matters independently from  
the stored text.  
  
## Mutation Semantics  
  
`Env::set` uses replacement semantics: if the variable already exists, its  
value is overwritten. `Env::unset` removes the name entirely. Both functions  
return `false` when the underlying platform call fails, for example because a  
name is invalid for the host C library.  
  
## Platform Notes  
  
These APIs are currently enabled on Linux and macOS. Changes affect only the  
current process and any children started after the change. Environment values  
are passed through POSIX `getenv(3)`, `setenv(3)`, and `unsetenv(3)`, so names  
and values must be representable as NUL-terminated C strings.  
  
## Example  
  
```ignis  
import Env from "std::env";  
  
function main(): i32 {  
  let home: Option<String> = Env::get("HOME");  
  return home.isSome() ? 0 : 1;  
}  
```

modules.doc:
# Display  
  
The `Display` trait and its implementations for the built-in types.  
  
`display` has a default that reflects over the record's fields with  
`comptime for`, so `@implements(Display)` on a record needs no method of  
its own. A `display` the record writes itself replaces the default.  
  
## Default  
  
`TypeName { field: value, field: value }`, fields in declaration order,  
each rendered by its own `Display`. The name is the record's concrete  
name: a generic record shows its type arguments, `Box<i32> { value: 1 }`.  
A record without fields renders as `TypeName {}`. A field whose type does  
not implement `Display` is a compile error inside the default, with a  
note naming the field.  
  
## Implementations  
  
| Type | Rendering |  
|------|-----------|  
| integers, `f32`, `f64`, `boolean` | `toString()`: `-3`, `1.5`, `true` |  
| `char` | the character itself, unquoted |  
| `str`, `String` | the text itself, unquoted and unescaped |  
| `Option<T: Display>` | `Option::SOME(value)` or `Option::NONE` |  
| `Vector<T: Display>` | `[first, second]`, `[]` when empty |  
  
## Enums  
  
The default walks record fields only. An enum that declares  
`@implements(Display)` without a `display` of its own is a compile error  
inside the default (A0293, `'@fields' needs a record`), so an enum  
needs a hand-written `display`.

# Filesystem System Layer  
  
Platform-specific syscall wrappers behind the common `Fs::Sys` namespace.  
  
This hub selects the correct platform backend at compile time via  
`@configFlag` directives. Each backend exports its API into `Fs::Sys`,  
so higher-level modules (`fs::file`, `fs::dir`, etc.) are platform-agnostic.  
  
## Backends  
  
| Source file | Platform       | Description                   |  
|------------|----------------|-------------------------------|  
| unix.ign   | Linux / macOS  | POSIX syscall wrappers        |

modules.name: std::fs::sys::unix
modules.doc:
# Unix Filesystem Syscall Layer  
  
Thin 1:1 wrappers around POSIX filesystem syscalls, returning  
`Result<T, Io::IoError>` instead of raw errno-based error codes.  
  
All public API lives under the `Fs::Sys` namespace.  
  
## Functions  
  
| Function   | Wraps              | Returns                           |  
|------------|--------------------|-----------------------------------|  
| `open`     | `open(2)` 3-arg    | `Result<i32, IoError>`            |  
| `close`    | `close(2)`         | `Result<void, IoError>`           |  
| `read`     | `read(2)`          | `Result<i64, IoError>`            |  
| `write`    | `write(2)`         | `Result<i64, IoError>`            |  
| `lseek`    | `lseek(2)`         | `Result<i64, IoError>`            |  
| `stat`     | `stat(2)`          | `Result<Stat, IoError>`           |  
| `fstat`    | `fstat(2)`         | `Result<Stat, IoError>`           |  
| `lstat`    | `lstat(2)`         | `Result<Stat, IoError>`           |  
| `realpath` | `realpath(3)`      | `Result<String, IoError>`         |  
| `tempDirPath` | env/stat fallback | `Result<String, IoError>`       |  
| `mkdir`    | `mkdir(2)`         | `Result<void, IoError>`           |  
| `unlink`   | `unlink(2)`        | `Result<void, IoError>`           |  
| `rmdir`    | `rmdir(2)`         | `Result<void, IoError>`           |  
| `removeDirAll` | recursive removal | `Result<void, IoError>`         |  
| `rename`   | `rename(2)`        | `Result<void, IoError>`           |  
| `opendir`  | `opendir(3)`       | `Result<DirPtr, IoError>`         |  
| `readdir`  | `readdir(3)`       | `Result<Option<SysDirEntry>, IoError>` |  
| `readdirEntry` | `readdir(3)`      | `Result<boolean, IoError>`      |  
| `closedir` | `closedir(3)`      | `void`                            |  
  
## Types  
  
| Type       | Description                                                   |  
|------------|---------------------------------------------------------------|  
| `Stat`         | File metadata: dev, ino, mode, nlink, uid, gid, size, times   |  
| `SysDirEntry`  | Directory entry: name (borrowed `str`), ino, fileType         |  
  
## Constants  
  
| Group          | Constants                                                    |  
|----------------|--------------------------------------------------------------|  
| Open flags     | `O_RDONLY`, `O_WRONLY`, `O_RDWR`, `O_CREAT`, `O_TRUNC`, ... |  
| Seek modes     | `SEEK_SET`, `SEEK_CUR`, `SEEK_END`                           |  
| File type mask | `S_IFMT`, `S_IFREG`, `S_IFDIR`, `S_IFLNK`                   |  
| Permission bits| `S_IRWXU`, `S_IRUSR`, `S_IWUSR`, ... (user/group/other)      |  
| Dirent types   | `DT_UNKNOWN`, `DT_REG`, `DT_DIR`, `DT_LNK`                  |  
  
## Design Notes  
  
Functions that succeed without a meaningful value (close, mkdir, etc.)  
return `Result<void, Io::IoError>` with `Result::OK(())`.  
  
## Host Layout Dependency  
  
Every function here calls libc directly through an Ignis `extern` block.  
Two of those calls read a struct whose layout is fixed by the target's  
kernel ABI rather than by POSIX:  
  
| Struct          | Read as                                              |  
|-----------------|------------------------------------------------------|  
| `struct stat`   | the `RawStat` record, laid out field for field       |  
| `struct dirent` | the `DIRENT_*` byte offsets, read through the pointer |  
  
Both are the x86_64 Linux layout and are gated on  
`@platform("linux") && @arch("x86_64")`. They exist only for that target,  
so a target whose layout has not been checked fails to compile instead of  
reading the wrong bytes; adding one means adding its layout under its own  
`@configFlag`.  
  
`open(2)` is variadic and Ignis has no variadic call syntax. No prototype is  
emitted for an `extern` declaration, so the fixed three-argument binding in  
`__fs_io` is compiled against the real declaration from `<fcntl.h>`.  
  
## Example  
  
```ignis  
import Fs from "std::fs";  
import Io from "std::io";  
  
function main(): i32 {  
  let fd: Result<i32, Io::IoError> = Fs::Sys::open(  
    "/tmp/test.txt",  
    Fs::Sys::O_WRONLY | Fs::Sys::O_CREAT | Fs::Sys::O_TRUNC,  
    438,  // 0o666  
  );  
  if fd.isError() { return 1; }  
  
  let rawFd: i32 = fd.unwrap();  
  let msg: *u8 = "hello from Ignis\n";  
  let n: Result<i64, Io::IoError> = Fs::Sys::write(rawFd, msg as *mut void, 17);  
  Fs::Sys::close(rawFd);  
  return 0;  
}  
```

modules.name: std::hash
modules.doc:
# Hash Module  
  
Deterministic hashing foundations for collections and user-defined keys.  
  
The default hasher uses 64-bit FNV-1a with a fixed offset basis and no  
randomized seeding. Hashes are therefore deterministic for a given stdlib  
and compiler version.  
  
`writeStr` hashes NUL-terminated `str` data.  
Owned `String` values should hash all owned bytes without routing through raw `toStr()`.

modules.name: std::http
modules.doc:
# HTTP  
  
HTTP/1.1 on the server side. The core is sans-IO: a request parser and a  
response serializer that never touch a socket. Anything that speaks HTTP  
but is not a web application (a proxy, a test harness, a server driver)  
builds on it. The parser receives bytes and returns what they mean; the  
serializer turns a response into bytes and leaves writing them to the  
caller. On top of it, `Http::Server` is a blocking driver that accepts  
connections and calls a handler with a request and a response.  
  
## Exports  
  
| Export                 | Description                                                          |  
|------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------|  
| `Http::RequestParser`  | `new(limits)`, `feed(&bytes)`, `feedStr(text)`, `next()`, `buffered()` |  
| `Http::ParseEvent`     | `NEED_MORE`, `HEAD(RequestHead)`, `BODY_CHUNK(Vector<u8>)`, `DONE`, `MALFORMED(ParseError)` |  
| `Http::RequestHead`    | `method`, `target`, `version`, `headers`; `keepAlive()`              |  
| `Http::Method`         | `GET`, `HEAD`, `POST`, `PUT`, `DELETE`, `PATCH`, `OPTIONS`, `CONNECT`, `TRACE`, `OTHER(String)`; `toString()` |  
| `Http::Version`        | `HTTP_1_0`, `HTTP_1_1`; `toStr()`                                    |  
| `Http::Headers`        | Ordered fields: `get`, `getAll`, `contains`, `hasToken`, `add`, `set`, `remove`, `length`, `nameAt`, `valueAt`, `fieldAt` |  
| `Http::HeaderField`    | One `name` and `value`                                               |  
| `Http::Limits`         | `maxRequestLine`, `maxHeaderLine`, `maxHeaders`, `maxBody`; `new()` gives the defaults |  
| `Http::ParseError`     | `kind` and the suggested response `status`                           |  
| `Http::ParseErrorKind` | Why a request is malformed; `name()`, `status()`                     |  
| `Http::ResponseHead`   | `status`, `reason`, `headers`; `create(status)`, `withReason(status, reason)` |  
| `Http::SerializeError` | Why a response head cannot be written                                |  
| `Http::writeHead`      | Appends a response head                                              |  
| `Http::writeResponse`  | Appends a head with `Content-Length` and the body                    |  
| `Http::writeBody`      | Appends body bytes unchanged                                         |  
| `Http::writeChunk`     | Appends one chunk of a chunked body                                  |  
| `Http::writeLastChunk` | Appends the chunk that ends a chunked body                           |  
| `Http::reasonPhrase`   | The standard reason phrase of a status                               |  
| `Http::Server`         | `bind(&address, config)`, `localAddress()`, `run(handler)`           |  
| `Http::ServerConfig`   | `threads`, `limits`, `idleTimeout`, `maxRequestsPerConnection`; `new()` gives the defaults |  
| `Http::Handler`        | Trait: `handle(&self, &Request, &mut Response)`                      |  
| `Http::Request`        | `head`, `body`; `target()`, `header(name)`, `bodyText()`             |  
| `Http::Response`       | `status`, `headers`, `body`; `new()`, `setStatus`, `setHeader`, `addHeader`, `write`, `writeStr` |  
| `Http::serveConnection` | Serves one connection with a handler                                |  
| `Http::acceptConnections` | Accepts and serves connections on the calling thread              |  
  
## Parsing  
  
`feed` copies bytes into the parser; `next` reports the next event. Each  
request produces `HEAD` once, zero or more `BODY_CHUNK`, then `DONE`.  
`NEED_MORE` means the bytes fed so far are not enough to report anything  
else. After `DONE` the parser starts on the next request of the same  
connection, and bytes already fed past the end of a request belong to the  
next one, so keep-alive and pipelining need nothing special.  
`RequestHead.keepAlive()` tells whether the connection stays open: an  
HTTP/1.1 request keeps it unless `Connection` lists `close`, an HTTP/1.0  
request closes it unless `Connection` lists `keep-alive`.  
  
Events own their payloads: a `RequestHead` or a body chunk is a copy and  
stays valid after more bytes are fed.  
  
`MALFORMED` is terminal: once the parser reports it, every later `next`  
reports the same error, because the rest of the connection cannot be  
framed. The `ParseError` carries the status a server should answer with  
(400, 413, 414, 431, 501 or 505) before it closes the connection.  
Malformed input never panics.  
  
## Message syntax  
  
- Lines end with CRLF. A bare LF is accepted too, as RFC 9112 section 2.2  
  allows a recipient to; a CR anywhere else is malformed.  
- Empty lines before a request line are skipped.  
- The request line is `method SP target SP HTTP/1.x` with exactly one space  
  between the parts. The method is a case-sensitive token; methods other  
  than the nine standard ones are `Method::OTHER`. The target is kept as  
  received and must be visible ASCII.  
- A version other than `HTTP/1.0` and `HTTP/1.1` is `UNSUPPORTED_VERSION`.  
- A header line is `name: value`. Whitespace between the name and the  
  colon, an obsolete line folding (a line starting with a space or a tab)  
  and a control byte in the value are `INVALID_HEADER`. Names keep their  
  casing; lookups ignore ASCII case.  
  
## Body framing  
  
Per RFC 9112 section 6.3:  
  
| Head                                   | Body                                           |  
|----------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------|  
| `Transfer-Encoding: chunked`           | Chunked; reported without the chunk framing    |  
| Any other `Transfer-Encoding`          | `UNSUPPORTED_TRANSFER_CODING` (501)            |  
| `Transfer-Encoding` and `Content-Length` | `CONFLICTING_LENGTH` (400), as request smuggling |  
| `Content-Length: n`                    | Exactly `n` bytes                              |  
| `Content-Length` values that disagree  | `CONFLICTING_LENGTH` (400)                     |  
| A `Content-Length` that is not a count | `INVALID_CONTENT_LENGTH` (400)                 |  
| Neither                                | No body                                        |  
  
Repeated `Content-Length` fields, or a comma list in one, are accepted when  
every value is the same. Chunk extensions are ignored. Trailer fields  
after the last chunk are checked like header fields, counted against  
`maxHeaders`, and discarded.  
  
## Limits  
  
| Limit            | Default   | Violation                                 |  
|------------------|-----------|-------------------------------------------|  
| `maxRequestLine` | 8192      | `REQUEST_LINE_TOO_LONG` (414)             |  
| `maxHeaderLine`  | 8192      | `HEADER_TOO_LONG` (431); `INVALID_CHUNK` for a chunk-size line |  
| `maxHeaders`     | 100       | `TOO_MANY_HEADERS` (431)                  |  
| `maxBody`        | 1048576   | `BODY_TOO_LARGE` (413)                    |  
  
Line lengths exclude the line terminator, and a length exactly at its  
limit is accepted. A line is rejected as soon as it grows past its limit,  
before it ends, and a body as soon as its declared size passes `maxBody`,  
so a client cannot make the parser buffer without bound.  
  
## Serializing  
  
`writeHead` appends `HTTP/1.1 <status> <reason>\r\n`, every header field  
and the blank line. `writeResponse` does the same with a `Content-Length`  
field and appends the body. For a chunked body, add  
`Transfer-Encoding: chunked` to the head, then call `writeChunk` for each  
piece and `writeLastChunk` at the end. A header name, header value or  
reason phrase holding CR or LF could split the response, so it is a  
`SerializeError` and nothing is appended.  
  
Byte inputs are `&Vector<u8>`: a slice parameter cannot report its length  
yet.  
  
## Serving  
  
A handler is a record that implements `Http::Handler`. Outside the `Http`  
namespace the trait is reached by its path: `@implements(Http::Handler)`.  
  
```ignis  
import Http from "std::http";  
import IpAddress, SocketAddress from "std::net";  
  
@implements(Http::Handler)  
record Greeter {  
  public greeting: str;  
  
  handle(&self, request: &Http::Request, response: &mut Http::Response): void {  
    if (!request.head.target.equals("/")) {  
      response.setStatus(404);  
      return;  
    }  
  
    response.setHeader("Content-Type", "text/plain");  
    response.writeStr(self.greeting);  
  }  
}  
  
function main(): i32 {  
  let address: SocketAddress = SocketAddress::create(IpAddress::v4(127, 0, 0, 1), 8080);  
  let Result::OK(server) = Http::Server::bind(&address, Http::ServerConfig::new()) else {  
    return 1;  
  };  
  
  return server.run<Greeter>(Greeter { greeting: "hello" }).isOk() ? 0 : 1;  
}  
```  
  
`run` starts `ServerConfig.threads` threads (default 8). Each accepts a  
connection, serves it to the end and accepts the next, so up to `threads`  
connections are served at once. The handler is shared by all of them,  
which is why it has to be `Send` and `Sync` and `handle` takes `&self`.  
`run` returns only once every thread's `accept` failed; there is no way  
to stop a running server yet, so it blocks for as long as the process  
lives.  
  
`acceptConnections` is the loop each `run` thread runs: it accepts a  
connection, serves it and accepts the next. Calling it on threads of  
your own gives every thread its own handler, for state that cannot be  
shared; `std::web` builds one router per thread this way.  
  
`serveConnection` serves one accepted connection on the calling thread,  
which is what each `run` thread does and what a test calls directly:  
  
- A request reaches the handler once its whole body is in, bounded by  
  `Limits.maxBody`. `Expect: 100-continue` is not answered: the client  
  sends the body after its own wait.  
- The response always carries `Content-Length`; a `Content-Length` or  
  `Transfer-Encoding` the handler set is dropped. A `HEAD` request gets  
  the head, with the length the body would have, and no body.  
- The connection stays open unless the request does not keep it alive  
  (`RequestHead.keepAlive`), the response lists `Connection: close`, or  
  `maxRequestsPerConnection` (0, no limit, by default) is reached. When  
  it closes, the response carries `Connection: close`.  
- Every read waits at most `idleTimeout` (default 30 seconds). When it  
  expires, or the client closes, the connection ends without a response.  
- A malformed request gets an empty response with the parser's status  
  and `Connection: close`, then the connection ends.  
- A response the serializer rejects, a status outside 100 to 999 or a  
  header that holds CR or LF, is replaced by an empty 500.  
- Before closing, the server shuts its writing side and discards what  
  the client still sends for up to 2 seconds, so the close does not reset  
  the connection before the client reads the response.  
  
## Example  
  
```ignis  
import Http from "std::http";  
  
function answer(request: str, out: &mut Vector<u8>): i32 {  
  let mut parser: Http::RequestParser = Http::RequestParser::new(Http::Limits::new());  
  parser.feedStr(request);  
  
  let Http::ParseEvent::HEAD(head) = parser.next() else {  
    return 1;  
  };  
  
  let mut response: Http::ResponseHead = Http::ResponseHead::create(200);  
  response.headers.add("Content-Type", "text/plain");  
  let body: Vector<u8> = head.target.toBytes();  
  
  return Http::writeResponse(&response, &body, out).isOk() ? 0 : 1;  
}  
```

modules.doc:
# I/O  
  
Standard output, error printing, structured I/O error types, buffered  
descriptor reads, and `Content-Length` message framing.  
  
All types and functions live under the `Io` namespace.  
  
## Printing  
  
| Function        | Stream   | Newline | Accepts          |  
|-----------------|----------|---------|------------------|  
| `Io::print`     | stdout   | No      | `String`         |  
| `Io::println`   | stdout   | Yes     | `String`, `str`  |  
| `Io::eprint`    | stderr   | No      | `String`         |  
| `Io::eprintln`  | stderr   | Yes     | `String`, `str`  |  
  
`println` and `eprintln` are overloaded for both `String` and `str`:  
- `String` overload: the value is consumed (moved), dropped after printing,  
  and writes `message.length()` bytes.  
- `str` overload: writes the C string directly, no heap allocation.  
  
`print` and `eprint` only accept `String` (no `str` overload).  
`String` overloads write `message.length()` bytes. `str` overloads remain  
NUL-terminated C-string writes and may stop at the first interior NUL.  
`str` overloads remain NUL-terminated C-string writes.  
  
## Error Types  
  
| Type              | Source file | Description                                      |  
|-------------------|------------|--------------------------------------------------|  
| `Io::ErrorKind`   | error.ign  | Category of the I/O error (14 variants)          |  
| `Io::IoError`     | error.ign  | Full error: kind + raw errno + strerror message  |  
  
## Streams and Framing  
  
| Item                        | Source file | Description                               |  
|-----------------------------|-------------|-------------------------------------------|  
| `Stream::ByteReader`         | stream.ign  | Buffered reader over a file descriptor    |  
| `Stream::ByteWriter`         | stream.ign  | Unbuffered whole-buffer writer            |  
| `Stream::ReadError`          | stream.ign  | End of input, truncation, or read failure |  
| `Stream::FrameError`         | stream.ign  | Why a framed message could not be read    |  
| `Stream::writeAll`           | stream.ign  | Write a whole `String` to a descriptor    |  
| `Stream::writeFramedMessage` | stream.ign  | Write a `Content-Length` framed message   |  
  
These live in the `Stream` namespace, re-exported here:  
`import Io, Stream from "std::io";`. `Stream::ByteReader::stdin()` reads  
standard input. `readFramedMessage` and  
`writeFramedMessage` implement the header framing the Language Server  
Protocol uses on stdin and stdout. `readFramedMessageWithin` does the same  
but skips, without buffering, a body longer than a caller-chosen limit.  
  
## Example  
  
```ignis  
import Io from "std::io";  
import LibC from "std::libc";  
  
function main(): i32 {  
  Io::println(String::create("hello, world!"));  
  
  // I/O error from a failed syscall  
  let fd: i32 = LibC::File::open("/nonexistent", LibC::File::O_RDONLY);  
  if (fd == -1) {  
    let err: Io::IoError = Io::IoError::lastError();  
    // err.kind == Io::ErrorKind::NOT_FOUND  
    // err.message == "No such file or directory"  
    return 1;  
  }  
  
  return 0;  
}  
```

modules.name: std::io::error
modules.doc:
# I/O Error Types  
  
Structured error types for I/O operations, exposed as `Io::ErrorKind`  
and `Io::IoError`.  
  
## Types  
  
| Type             | Description                                          |  
|------------------|------------------------------------------------------|  
| `Io::ErrorKind`  | Category of the I/O error (enum, 14 variants)        |  
| `Io::IoError`    | Full error: kind + raw errno + human-readable message |  
  
## ErrorKind Variants  
  
| Variant             | Errno            | Description                          |  
|---------------------|------------------|--------------------------------------|  
| `NOT_FOUND`         | `ENOENT`         | No such file or directory            |  
| `PERMISSION_DENIED` | `EACCES`         | Permission denied                    |  
| `ALREADY_EXISTS`    | `EEXIST`         | File or resource already exists      |  
| `INVALID_INPUT`     | `EINVAL`         | Invalid argument                     |  
| `INTERRUPTED`       | `EINTR`          | Operation interrupted by signal      |  
| `WOULD_BLOCK`       | `EAGAIN`         | Resource temporarily unavailable     |  
| `TIMED_OUT`         | `ETIMEDOUT`      | Connection or operation timed out    |  
| `CONNECTION_REFUSED`| `ECONNREFUSED`   | Nothing listens at the remote address |  
| `CONNECTION_RESET`  | `ECONNRESET`     | The peer reset the connection        |  
| `ADDRESS_IN_USE`    | `EADDRINUSE`     | Local address already bound          |  
| `ADDRESS_NOT_AVAILABLE` | `EADDRNOTAVAIL` | Local address not owned by this host |  
| `BROKEN_PIPE`       | `EPIPE`          | Write to a pipe or socket the peer closed |  
| `NOT_CONNECTED`     | `ENOTCONN`       | Socket is not connected              |  
| `OTHER`             | anything else    | Unmapped errno value                 |  
  
## Construction  
  
| Method                         | Description                              |  
|--------------------------------|------------------------------------------|  
| `Io::IoError::fromErrno(raw)`  | Map raw errno to kind + strerror message |  
| `Io::IoError::lastError()`     | Read thread-local errno, then fromErrno  |  
  
## Example  
  
```ignis  
import Io from "std::io";  
import LibC from "std::libc";  
  
function main(): i32 {  
  let fd: i32 = LibC::File::open("/nonexistent", LibC::File::O_RDONLY);  
  if (fd == -1) {  
    let err: Io::IoError = Io::IoError::lastError();  
    // err.kind == Io::ErrorKind::NOT_FOUND  
    // err.raw  == 2  (ENOENT)  
    // err.message == "No such file or directory"  
    return 1;  
  }  
  return 0;  
}  
```

modules.doc:
# JSON  
  
JSON serialization front-end for the shared `std::serializer` contracts.  
  
## Overview  
  
The `Json` namespace configures `Serializer::Writer` for JSON object syntax  
and exposes `writeRoot` overloads for scalar and `Serialize` values. Output is  
appended to a caller-provided `String`.  
  
JSON is the permissive front-end for the shared serializer: scalar document  
roots are allowed, field names are always quoted, and record entries are  
separated with commas.  
  
```text  
  Json::writer()  
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐  
  │ recordPrefix: "{"                            │  
  │ recordSuffix: "}"                            │  
  │ entrySeparator: ","                          │  
  │ fieldSeparator: ":"                          │  
  │ supportsScalarRoot: true                     │  
  │ quoteFieldKeys: true                         │  
  │ nestedRecordPrefix: "{"                      │  
  │ nestedRecordSuffix: "}"                      │  
  │ nestedEntrySeparator: ","                    │  
  │ depth: 0                                     │  
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘  
```  
  
## APIs  
  
| Function            | Description                                      |  
|---------------------|--------------------------------------------------|  
| `Json::writer`      | JSON writer configuration                        |  
| `Json::writeRoot`   | Serialize a root scalar or `Serialize` value     |  
| `Json::parse`       | Parse JSON text into a `JsonValue` tree          |  
| `Json::writeValue`  | Append a `JsonValue` tree as compact JSON        |  
| `Json::writeValuePretty` | Append a `JsonValue` tree as pretty JSON    |  
| `Json::toJsonString` | Compact JSON for a `JsonValue` tree             |  
| `Json::toJsonStringPretty` | Pretty JSON for a `JsonValue` tree        |  
  
## Notes  
  
JSON supports scalar roots, quotes field keys, and uses comma-separated  
object entries. String escaping is provided by the shared serializer helpers.  
`writeRoot` appends to the provided output string, while `stringify` creates a  
fresh output string and returns it.  
  
## Root Shapes  
  
| Root value                    | Supported | Notes                       |  
|-------------------------------|-----------|-----------------------------|  
| Boolean, number, char, string | Yes       | Uses scalar overloads        |  
| `T: Serialize`                | Yes       | Uses record serialization    |  
| `JsonValue` (any shape)       | Yes       | Uses `Json::writeValue`      |  
  
## JSON Values  
  
A `JsonValue` tree holds any JSON document: null, booleans, numbers,  
strings, arrays, and objects with keys kept in insertion order. `Json::parse`  
builds one from text, and the `JsonValue` static constructors (`nullValue`,  
`boolValue`, `stringValue`, `fromString`, `integerValue`, `unsignedValue`,  
`array`, `object`) build one in code.  
  
| Value shape                   | Build | Parse | Write |  
|-------------------------------|-------|-------|-------|  
| Null, boolean, string         | Yes   | Yes   | Yes   |  
| Integers (`i64`, `u64`)       | Yes   | Yes   | Yes   |  
| Floats                        | No    | Yes   | Yes   |  
| Arrays                        | Yes   | Yes   | Yes   |  
| Objects (ordered keys)        | Yes   | Yes   | Yes   |  
  
Parsed numbers keep their source text, so a parsed float is written back  
unchanged. There is no float constructor because `f64.toString()` uses  
C `%g` formatting (six significant digits, `42.0` as `42`), which neither  
round-trips nor matches the text `serde_json` writes.  
  
`Json::writeValue` and `Json::writeValuePretty` match `serde_json::to_string`  
and `serde_json::to_string_pretty` byte for byte, string escaping included.  
The scalar `writeRoot` overloads use the shared serializer escaping instead,  
which writes other control bytes as uppercase `\u00XX` and has no `\b` or  
`\f`.  
  
## Example  
  
```ignis  
import Json from "std::json";  
  
function main(): i32 {  
  let mut output: String = String::create("");  
  Json::writeRoot(&output, true);  
  return 0;  
}  
```

modules.name: std::json::parser
modules.doc:
A JSON value parser, `serde_json`-shaped on the errors it reports:  
`Json::parse` exists so a consumer that has to match a `serde` host's  
exact wording (`ignis/format`'s `--stdin-json` protocol is the one that  
does) can build one on top of a real parse tree instead of a hand-rolled  
scanner that only sees quotes.  
  
This is not a general-purpose JSON library: writing a tree lives in  
`./writer` (`Json::writeValue`), and there is no streaming API. It implements  
the full JSON grammar (RFC 8259) for values, strings (including `\uXXXX`  
surrogate pairs), and numbers, and reports the same messages `serde_json`  
does for the malformed shapes this module's tests, and  
`ignis/format/api_tests.ign`, pin against the host binary.  
  
`Format::parseStdinRequest` does not build a `JsonValue` tree through  
`Json::parse` for its own top-level object scan: a `serde`-derived struct  
deserializer inspects a field's value shallowly (peeking whether it is a  
string without descending into it when it is not) and skips an unknown  
field's value iteratively (no recursion, so no depth limit) rather than  
building a tree first and type-checking after. Reproducing that ordering  
needs the lower-level pieces this module exports (`readString`,  
`scanNumber`, `skipValue`, `classifyContainerStart`) directly, which is  
also why those are exported rather than kept private to `Json::parse`.

modules.name: std::json::value
modules.doc:
The value tree `Json::parse` builds, and nothing else: this module has no  
opinion on how a caller maps a `JsonValue` onto its own record types.

modules.name: std::json::writer
modules.doc:
Writes a `JsonValue` tree back out as JSON text, byte-compatible with  
`serde_json`: `Json::toJsonString` matches `serde_json::to_string` and  
`Json::toJsonStringPretty` matches `serde_json::to_string_pretty`.  
  
`NUMBER` payloads are written as their stored text, unchanged. A tree from  
`Json::parse` or the `JsonValue` integer constructors always holds valid  
number text; a caller building `JsonValueKind::NUMBER` by hand owns that.

std::libc::errno
modules.doc:
# LibC Errno  
  
Thread-local `errno` access and POSIX error constants, exposed as  
`LibC::Errno`.  
  
## Functions  
  
| Function | Description                                         |  
|----------|-----------------------------------------------------|  
| `get`    | Read the current thread-local `errno` value         |  
| `set`    | Write a new value into thread-local `errno`         |  
  
## Error Constants  
  
Every error constant comes from `std::libc::platform`: written out on  
`x86_64` Linux, read from `<errno.h>` on other targets.  
  
| Constant       | Description                        |  
|----------------|------------------------------------|  
| `EPERM`        | Operation not permitted            |  
| `ENOENT`       | No such file or directory          |  
| `ESRCH`        | No such process                    |  
| `EINTR`        | Interrupted system call            |  
| `EIO`          | I/O error                          |  
| `ENXIO`        | No such device or address          |  
| `E2BIG`        | Argument list too long             |  
| `EACCES`       | Permission denied                  |  
| `EBADF`        | Bad file descriptor                |  
| `EAGAIN`       | Resource temporarily unavailable   |  
| `ENOMEM`       | Cannot allocate memory             |  
| `EBUSY`        | Resource busy                      |  
| `EEXIST`       | File exists                        |  
| `ENOTDIR`      | Not a directory                    |  
| `EISDIR`       | Is a directory                     |  
| `EINVAL`       | Invalid argument                   |  
| `ENFILE`       | Too many open files in system      |  
| `EMFILE`       | Too many open files (per process)  |  
| `ENOSPC`       | No space left on device            |  
| `EROFS`        | Read-only file system              |  
| `EPIPE`        | Broken pipe                        |  
| `ERANGE`       | Result too large (math)            |  
| `ENOTEMPTY`    | Directory not empty                |  
| `ECONNREFUSED` | Connection refused                 |  
| `ECONNRESET`   | Connection reset by peer           |  
| `ETIMEDOUT`    | Connection timed out               |  
| `EWOULDBLOCK`  | Alias for `EAGAIN`                 |  
  
## Platform Notes  
  
On Linux/glibc, `errno` is a macro expanding to `(*__errno_location())`.  
The `get` and `set` functions call `__errno_location` to read/write the  
thread-local value.  
  
## Example  
  
```ignis  
import LibC, CType from "std::libc";  
  
function main(): i32 {  
  let fd: CType::CInt = LibC::File::open("/nonexistent", LibC::File::O_RDONLY);  
  if fd == -1 {  
    let err: CType::CInt = LibC::Errno::get();  
    if err == LibC::Errno::ENOENT {  
      // file not found -- expected  
      return 0;  
    }  
  }  
  return 1;  
}  
```

modules.name: std::libc::io
modules.doc:
# LibC I/O  
  
POSIX file-descriptor operations from `unistd.h`, `fcntl.h` and `sys/ioctl.h`,  
exposed as `LibC::File`.  
  
## Constants  
  
| Constant         | Description                       |  
|------------------|-----------------------------------|  
| `SEEK_SET`       | Seek from beginning of file       |  
| `SEEK_CUR`       | Seek from current position        |  
| `SEEK_END`       | Seek from end of file             |  
| `STDIN_FILENO`   | Standard input fd (0)             |  
| `STDOUT_FILENO`  | Standard output fd (1)            |  
| `STDERR_FILENO`  | Standard error fd (2)             |  
| `O_RDONLY`       | Open for reading only             |  
| `O_WRONLY`       | Open for writing only             |  
| `O_RDWR`         | Open for reading and writing      |  
| `O_CREAT`        | Create file if it does not exist  |  
| `O_TRUNC`        | Truncate file to zero length      |  
| `O_APPEND`       | Append on each write              |  
| `F_GETFD`        | `fcntl` request: get fd flags     |  
| `F_SETFD`        | `fcntl` request: set fd flags     |  
| `FD_CLOEXEC`     | Close fd on successful `exec`     |  
  
## Functions  
  
| Function  | Description                                        |  
|-----------|----------------------------------------------------|  
| `open`    | Open file by pathname                              |  
| `close`   | Close file descriptor                              |  
| `read`    | Read bytes from file descriptor                    |  
| `write`   | Write bytes to file descriptor                     |  
| `lseek`   | Reposition file offset                             |  
| `unlink`  | Delete filesystem name                             |  
| `rmdir`   | Remove empty directory                             |  
| `getcwd`  | Get current working directory                      |  
| `chdir`   | Change working directory                           |  
| `dup`     | Duplicate file descriptor                          |  
| `dup2`    | Duplicate fd to specific number                    |  
| `isatty`  | Test if fd refers to a terminal                    |  
| `fcntl`   | Run `fcntl(fd, cmd)`                               |  
| `fcntlArg`| Run `fcntl(fd, cmd, arg)`                          |  
| `windowSize` | Read a terminal's size (`TIOCGWINSZ`)           |  
  
Most functions return -1 on error. `read` returns 0 on EOF.  
  
## Example  
  
```ignis  
import LibC, CType from "std::libc";  
  
function main(): i32 {  
  let fd: CType::CInt = LibC::File::open(  
    "hello.txt",  
    LibC::File::O_WRONLY | LibC::File::O_CREAT | LibC::File::O_TRUNC,  
  );  
  if fd == -1 {  
    return 1;  
  }  
  let data: *u8 = "hello, world\n";  
  LibC::File::write(fd, data as CType::CConstVoidPtr, 13);  
  LibC::File::close(fd);  
  return 0;  
}  
```

modules.doc:
The C platform constants the standard library uses, in one place.  
  
On `x86_64` Linux every value is written here, so no backend needs a C  
header to know it. `scripts/check_platform_constants.py` compiles each

# C Primitive Types  
  
Raw C ABI type aliases used by `std::libc`.  
  
## Type Mapping  
  
| C Type                | Ignis Alias           | Ignis Base | Size  |  
|-----------------------|-----------------------|------------|-------|  
| `char`                | `CType::CChar`        | `u8`       | 1     |  
| `signed char`         | `CType::CSChar`       | `i8`       | 1     |  
| `unsigned char`       | `CType::CUChar`       | `u8`       | 1     |  
| `short`               | `CType::CShort`       | `i16`      | 2     |  
| `unsigned short`      | `CType::CUShort`      | `u16`      | 2     |  
| `int`                 | `CType::CInt`         | `i32`      | 4     |  
| `unsigned int`        | `CType::CUInt`        | `u32`      | 4     |  
| `long`                | `CType::CLong`        | `i64`      | 8 *   |  
| `unsigned long`       | `CType::CULong`       | `u64`      | 8 *   |  
| `long long`           | `CType::CLongLong`    | `i64`      | 8     |  
| `unsigned long long`  | `CType::CULongLong`   | `u64`      | 8     |  
| `float`               | `CType::CFloat`       | `f32`      | 4     |  
| `double`              | `CType::CDouble`      | `f64`      | 8     |  
| `size_t`              | `CType::SizeT`        | `u64`      | 8     |  
| `ssize_t`             | `CType::SSizeT`       | `i64`      | 8     |  
| `ptrdiff_t`           | `CType::PtrDiffT`     | `i64`      | 8     |  
| `intptr_t`            | `CType::IntPtrT`      | `i64`      | 8     |  
| `uintptr_t`           | `CType::UIntPtrT`     | `u64`      | 8     |  
| `void*`               | `CType::CVoidPtr`     | `*mut void`| 8     |  
| `const void*`         | `CType::CConstVoidPtr`| `*void`    | 8     |  
| `char*`               | `CType::CStr`         | `*mut u8`  | 8     |  
| `const char*`         | `CType::CConstStr`    | `*u8`      | 8     |  
| `pid_t`               | `CType::PidT`         | `i32`      | 4     |  
| `uid_t`               | `CType::UidT`         | `u32`      | 4     |  
| `gid_t`               | `CType::GidT`         | `u32`      | 4     |  
| `off_t`               | `CType::OffT`         | `i64`      | 8     |  
| `mode_t`              | `CType::ModeT`        | `u32`      | 4     |  
| `dev_t`               | `CType::DevT`         | `u64`      | 8     |  
| `ino_t`               | `CType::InoT`         | `u64`      | 8     |  
| `nlink_t`             | `CType::NlinkT`       | `u64`      | 8     |  
| `blksize_t`           | `CType::BlkSizeT`     | `i64`      | 8     |  
| `blkcnt_t`            | `CType::BlkCntT`      | `i64`      | 8     |  
| `DIR*`                | `CType::DirPtr`       | `*mut void`| 8     |  
| `time_t`              | `CType::TimeT`        | `i64`      | 8     |  
| `clock_t`             | `CType::ClockT`       | `i64`      | 8     |  
  
(*) `long` is 8 bytes on LP64 (Linux/macOS 64-bit) but 4 bytes on LLP64  
(Windows 64-bit). These aliases assume LP64.  
  
## Platform Assumption  
  
Type sizes match LP64 targets (Linux/macOS 64-bit).  
`long`-related aliases differ on LLP64 platforms.  
  
## Example  
  
```ignis  
import CType from "std::libc/primitives";  
  
function main(): i32 {  
  let n: CType::SizeT = 128;  
  let p: CType::CVoidPtr = null;  
  let ok: boolean = p == CType::NULL;  
  return ok ? (n as i32) : 0;  
}  
```

# LibC Process  
  
Process control, signals, and child process management.  
  
## Sub-namespaces  
  
| Namespace        | C Header               | Description                           |  
|------------------|------------------------|---------------------------------------|  
| `LibC::Process`  | `stdlib.h`, `unistd.h` | Process lifecycle, environment, IPC, exec |  
| `LibC::Signals`  | `signal.h`             | `raise`, `kill`                       |  
| `LibC::Wait`     | `sys/wait.h`           | `wait`, `waitpid`                     |  
  
## Constants  
  
| Namespace        | Constant         | Description                       |  
|------------------|------------------|-----------------------------------|  
| `LibC::Process`  | `EXIT_SUCCESS`   | Successful exit status            |  
| `LibC::Process`  | `EXIT_FAILURE`   | Failure exit status               |  
| `LibC::Signals`  | `SIGINT`         | Interrupt from keyboard (Ctrl-C)  |  
| `LibC::Signals`  | `SIGKILL`        | Kill signal (cannot be caught)    |  
| `LibC::Signals`  | `SIGSEGV`        | Segmentation fault                |  
| `LibC::Signals`  | `SIGTERM`        | Termination signal                |  
  
## Process Functions  
  
| Function       | Description                                      |  
|----------------|--------------------------------------------------|  
| `fork`         | Duplicate the current process                    |  
| `pipe`         | Create a unidirectional file-descriptor pair     |  
| `execvp`       | Replace the process image using PATH lookup      |  
| `setenv`       | Set or replace a process environment variable    |  
| `unsetenv`     | Remove a process environment variable            |  
  
## Example  
  
```ignis  
import LibC, CType from "std::libc";  
  
function main(): i32 {  
  let pid: CType::PidT = LibC::Process::getpid();  
  let home: CType::CStr = LibC::Process::getenv("HOME");  
  
  if home == null {  
    LibC::Process::exit(LibC::Process::EXIT_FAILURE);  
  }  
  
  return 0;  
}  
```

# LibC Stdio  
  
Buffered stream I/O from `stdio.h`, exposed as `LibC::Stdio`.  
  
These operate on opaque `FILE*` streams (`CType::FilePtr`), in contrast  
to the raw file-descriptor operations in `LibC::File` (`unistd.h`).  
  
## Constants  
  
| Constant    | Description                             |  
|-------------|-----------------------------------------|  
| `SEEK_SET`  | Seek from beginning of file             |  
| `SEEK_CUR`  | Seek from current position              |  
| `SEEK_END`  | Seek from end of file                   |  
| `EOF`       | End-of-file / error indicator (-1)      |  
  
## Functions  
  
| Function    | Description                                       |  
|-------------|---------------------------------------------------|  
| `fopen`     | Open file by pathname, returns stream              |  
| `fdopen`    | Associate stream with existing file descriptor     |  
| `fclose`    | Close stream                                      |  
| `fread`     | Read binary data from stream                      |  
| `fwrite`    | Write binary data to stream                       |  
| `fgets`     | Read line (up to newline or EOF)                   |  
| `fputs`     | Write null-terminated string to stream             |  
| `fseek`     | Set stream position                               |  
| `ftell`     | Get current stream position                       |  
| `rewind`    | Reset stream to beginning                         |  
| `fflush`    | Flush buffered output                             |  
| `feof`      | Test end-of-file indicator                        |  
| `ferror`    | Test error indicator                              |  
| `remove`    | Delete file by pathname                           |  
| `rename`    | Rename file                                       |  
| `mkstemp`   | Create and open a unique temporary file           |  
| `snprintfDouble` | Format one `double` into a sized buffer      |  
  
## Variadic functions  
  
`snprintf` is variadic, and Ignis has no variadic call syntax. Each argument  
shape it is used with gets its own fixed-arity binding here, named after the  
argument it takes. The declaration is only the Ignis-side type: the emitted  
call is compiled against the real prototype from `stdio.h`, so the host's  
variadic call sequence is what the C compiler generates.  
  
## Example  
  
```ignis  
import LibC, CType from "std::libc";  
  
function main(): i32 {  
  let fp: CType::FilePtr = LibC::Stdio::fopen("log.txt", "w");  
  if fp == null {  
    return 1;  
  }  
  
  LibC::Stdio::fputs("line one\n", fp);  
  LibC::Stdio::fputs("line two\n", fp);  
  LibC::Stdio::fflush(fp);  
  
  // Seek back to the beginning and overwrite  
  LibC::Stdio::fseek(fp, 0, LibC::Stdio::SEEK_SET);  
  LibC::Stdio::fputs("REPLACED\n", fp);  
  
  LibC::Stdio::fclose(fp);  
  return 0;  
}  
```
