modules.name: std::serializer::core
modules.doc:
# Serializer Core  
  
Format-agnostic serializer helpers shared by front-ends and user records.  
  
## Overview  
  
Core helpers implement the state-free operations needed by JSON and TOML  
serialization: opening and closing records, writing field names, escaping text,  
validating bare keys, and appending scalar text. The caller owns all ordering  
decisions; this module only appends the requested bytes to the destination.  
  
## Record Emission Flow  
  
A typical `Serialize` implementation uses these helpers in this order:  
  
```text  
  beginRecord(output, writer)  
       │  
       ├─ writeField(output, "first", writer, true)  
       │       └─ Serializer::write(output, value, writer)  
       │  
       ├─ writeField(output, "second", writer, false)  
       │       └─ Serializer::write(output, value, writer)  
       │  
       └─ endRecord(output, writer)  
```  
  
The `first` flag controls whether the writer's entry separator is emitted  
before a field. The core helpers do not track field count internally.  
  
## Nested Records  
  
A writer carries its `depth`: `0` for the root record, one more for each  
enclosing record. `beginRecord`, `writeField` and `endRecord` use the root  
punctuation at depth `0` and the `nested*` punctuation below it, which is  
how TOML writes a root document but an inline table for a nested record.  
A record passes `Serializer::nested(writer)` to the value of a field; the  
depth travels in the writer value, so a helper that fails part-way leaves  
no state behind.  
  
## Escaping  
  
`writeQuotedString` and `writeQuotedChar` use byte-oriented escaping. Quotes,  
backslashes, newlines, carriage returns, tabs, and ASCII control bytes are  
escaped. Other bytes are written through as UTF-8 bytes stored in Ignis  
`String` values.

modules.name: std::serializer::error
modules.doc:
# Serializer Errors  
  
Shared structured error types for std serialization entrypoints.  
  
## Overview  
  
Serializer errors are format-neutral. Front-ends such as `std::json` and  
`std::toml` return the same error type so callers can handle serialization  
failures without depending on a concrete writer implementation.  
  
## Error Kinds  
  
| Kind                       | Meaning                                      |  
|----------------------------|----------------------------------------------|  
| `UNSUPPORTED_ROOT_SHAPE`   | The format rejected the requested root value  |  
| `INVALID_FIELD_KEY`        | A record field key cannot be emitted safely   |  
  
Error messages are human-readable diagnostics. Match on `kind` for program  
control flow.

modules.name: std::serializer::serialize
modules.doc:
# Serializer Trait  
  
Shared format-agnostic record serialization contract.  
  
## Overview  
  
`Serialize` is implemented by records that know how to write their own fields  
into a caller-provided `String` using a caller-provided `Serializer::Writer`.  
The trait does not choose a format; JSON, TOML, or another front-end supplies  
the writer configuration.  
  
## Exports  
  
| Export      | Description                                                 |  
|-------------|-------------------------------------------------------------|  
| `Serialize` | `serialize(&self, output, writer)`, with a reflective record default and implementations for the scalar types |  
  
## Default  
  
`serialize` has a default that reflects over the record's fields with  
`comptime for`, so `@implements(Serialize)` on a record needs no method of  
its own. It writes `beginRecord`, then one `writeField` and value per  
field in declaration order, then `endRecord`. The key is the name given by  
`@Serializer::Rename("key")` on the field, else the field name. Each value  
is written by its type's `Serialize`:  
  
| Field type | Written by |  
|------------|------------|  
| `boolean`, integers, `f32`, `f64`, `char`, `str`, `String` | the matching `Serializer::write` overload |  
| a record implementing `Serialize` | its own `serialize`, as a nested record |  
  
A field of any other type, `Option` and `Vector` included, is a compile  
error inside the default, with a note naming the field: the writer has no  
null or array output yet. Each field value is written with  
`Serializer::nested(writer)`, so a nested record takes the writer's nested  
punctuation: an object in JSON, an inline table in TOML  
(`owner = { name = "Ada", age = 36 }`), recursively. A `serialize` the  
record writes itself replaces the default.  
  
The default walks record fields only. An enum that declares  
`@implements(Serialize)` without a `serialize` of its own is a compile  
error inside the default (A0293, `'@fields' needs a record`), so an enum  
needs a hand-written `serialize`.  
  
## Contract  
  
Implementations should:  
  
- Append output to the provided `String` without clearing it.  
- Call `Serializer::beginRecord` before emitting fields.  
- Call `Serializer::writeField` before each field value.  
- Pass `first = true` only for the first field.  
- Use `Serializer::write` for scalar field values, and pass  
  `Serializer::nested(writer)` to the `serialize` of a nested record.  
- Propagate `Serializer::Error` with `!` when a helper fails.  
- Call `Serializer::endRecord` before returning success.  
  
```ignis  
import Serialize, Serializer from "std::serializer";  
  
record Package {  
  name: String;  
  
  public serialize(&self, output: &mut String, writer: &Serializer::Writer): Result<boolean, Serializer::Error> {  
    Serializer::beginRecord(output, writer)!;  
    Serializer::writeField(output, "name", writer, true)!;  
    Serializer::write(output, &self.name, writer)!;  
    Serializer::endRecord(output, writer)!;  
  
    return Result::OK(true);  
  }  
}  
```

modules.name: std::serializer::writer
modules.doc:
# Serializer Writer  
  
Shared writer configuration used by concrete format frontends.  
  
## Overview  
  
This module provides scalar `Serializer::write` overloads for primitive Ignis  
values. The overloads append text to an existing output string using the  
selected writer's escaping and field-key policy.  
  
## Scalar Output Rules  
  
| Value kind           | Output behavior                                  |  
|----------------------|--------------------------------------------------|  
| `boolean`            | Writes `true` or `false`                         |  
| integers/floats      | Writes `toString()` output without quotes        |  
| `char`               | Writes a quoted, escaped one-byte character      |  
| `str` / `String`     | Writes a quoted, escaped string                  |  
  
Scalar overloads do not inspect `supportsScalarRoot`; root-shape validation is  
the responsibility of concrete front-ends such as `Toml::writeRoot`.  
  
## Common Contract For `Serializer::write`  
  
Every overload follows the same contract:  
  
- append to `output`; never clear existing content  
- use `writer` only for formatting policy that affects this value kind  
- return `Result::OK(true)` when text was appended successfully  
- return `Serializer::Error` only for format rules that can be violated  
  
Numeric and boolean overloads cannot currently fail because they only append  
`toString()` output. String and character overloads also currently cannot fail  
because escaping is total for byte-backed UTF-8 strings.  
  
## Usage Pattern  
  
Concrete front-ends call these overloads after selecting a writer:  
  
```ignis  
import Json from "std::json";  
import Serializer from "std::serializer";  
  
let writer: Serializer::Writer = Json::writer();  
let mut output: String = String::new();  
Serializer::write(&mut output, 42, &writer)!;  
```

modules.name: std::sqlite3
modules.doc:
# SQLite3  
  
A faithful SQLite binding: `std::sqlite3` wraps the C API's `sqlite3*` and  
`sqlite3_stmt*` handles in RAII types and returns every failure as a  
`Result`. The mapping layer, `std::orm`, builds on it; programs that only  
want raw SQL never link anything else.  
  
## Exports  
  
| Export                | Description                                    |  
|-----------------------|------------------------------------------------|  
| `Sqlite3::Connection` | One database: `open`, `openInMemory`, `close`, `exec`, `prepare`, `lastInsertRowId`, `changes`, `busyTimeout`, `begin`. Closes on drop |  
| `Sqlite3::Statement`  | One compiled statement: `bindNull`, `bindInt`, `bindReal`, `bindText`, `bindBlob`, `step`, `columnCount`, `columnIsNull`, `columnInt`, `columnReal`, `columnText`, `columnBlob`, `reset`. Finalizes on drop |  
| `Sqlite3::Step`       | `ROW` or `DONE`, what `Statement::step` reports |  
| `Sqlite3::Transaction`| A scoped transaction: `commit`, `rollback`; rolls back on drop |  
| `Sqlite3::Error`      | `code` (extended result code) and `message`; `isConstraint()` |  
  
## Errors  
  
Every fallible operation returns `Result<T, Sqlite3::Error>`; nothing in  
the module panics. `Error::code` is SQLite's extended result code and  
`Error::isConstraint()` names the constraint family, which a service turns  
into 409/422. See `std::sqlite3::error`.  
  
## Linking  
  
The module links `libsqlite3` and includes `sqlite3.h`  
(`[linking.sqlite3]` in `std/manifest.toml`), so every machine that builds  
the compiler or the standard library needs the SQLite development headers  
installed (`libsqlite3-dev` on Debian and Ubuntu, `pkgs.sqlite` in this  
repository's Nix dev shell).  
  
## Journal mode  
  
`Connection::open` runs `PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL` on file databases so  
readers do not block behind a writer; `":memory:"` databases skip the  
pragma, where WAL never applies. See `std::sqlite3::connection`.  
  
## Example  
  
```ignis  
import Sqlite3 from "std::sqlite3";  
  
function main(): i32 {  
  let mut connection: Sqlite3::Connection = Sqlite3::Connection::openInMemory().unwrap();  
  
  connection.exec("CREATE TABLE tasks (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, title TEXT NOT NULL)").unwrap();  
  
  let mut statement: Sqlite3::Statement =  
    connection.prepare("INSERT INTO tasks (title) VALUES (?)").unwrap();  
  
  statement.bindText(1, "write the ORM").unwrap();  
  statement.step().unwrap();  
  
  return connection.lastInsertRowId() == 1 ? 0 : 1;  
}  
```  
  
## Statements  
  
`Connection::prepare` compiles only the first statement of its SQL;  
anything after the first semicolon is not compiled and is silently  
dropped. Run each statement on its own `prepare`, or hand multi-statement  
scripts that need no parameters and read no rows to `Connection::exec`.  
  
## Transactions  
  
`Connection::begin` returns a `Sqlite3::Transaction` that commits on  
`commit()` and rolls back on drop, so an early `return` cannot leave one  
open; the guard reads its connection's live handle on every use, so a  
transaction on a closed connection is refused with a misuse error instead  
of touching freed memory. See `std::sqlite3::transaction`.  
  
## Non-goals  
  
The binding is blocking and synchronous. There is no asynchronous API and  
no query builder; the mapping layer is `std::orm`, not this module.

modules.name: std::sqlite3::connection
modules.doc:
# Connection  
  
`Sqlite3::Connection`, one open SQLite database. Owns the `sqlite3*`  
handle and closes it on drop; `close()` does the same thing early and  
reports the result.  
  
## Construction  
  
| Method           | Description                                       |  
|------------------|---------------------------------------------------|  
| `Connection::open(path)` | Opens (or creates) the database file `path` |  
| `Connection::openInMemory()` | Opens a private `:memory:` database     |  
  
Both run `PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL` on a file database so readers do not  
block behind a writer; SQLite silently keeps the previous journal mode  
where the filesystem cannot support WAL, and `open` still succeeds. An  
in-memory database skips the pragma: WAL never applies to `:memory:`, and  
only the exact path `":memory:"` is recognized as one.  
  
## Errors  
  
Every fallible operation returns `Result<T, Sqlite3::Error>`. The error's  
`code` is the extended result code and `message` is what `sqlite3_errmsg`  
reports; see `std::sqlite3::error`.  
  
## Threading  
  
A `Connection` holds a raw `sqlite3*`, so it is not `Send`, and a  
`Mutex<Connection>` does not compile: `Mutex` requires `Send`. To share one  
connection between threads, wrap it in `Sqlite3::SharedConnection` and put  
that behind a `Mutex` (`Shared<Sqlite3::SharedConnection>`):  
  
```ignis  
let cell: Sqlite3::SharedConnection = Sqlite3::SharedConnection::new(connection);  
let shared: Shared<Sqlite3::SharedConnection> = Arc::new<Mutex<Sqlite3::SharedConnection>>(Mutex::new<Sqlite3::SharedConnection>(cell));  
let mut guard: MutexGuard<Sqlite3::SharedConnection> = shared.get().lock();  
guard.get().connection.exec("INSERT INTO t VALUES (1)").unwrap();  
```  
  
The handle may then move between threads, one at a time. A `Statement` or  
`Transaction` taken through the guard must not outlive the guard.

modules.name: std::sqlite3::error
modules.doc:
# Errors  
  
`Sqlite3::Error`, the error type every fallible operation of `std::sqlite3`  
returns. Nothing in the module panics: a failing SQLite call becomes an  
`Error` value carrying the extended result code and the message that  
`sqlite3_errmsg` reports for the connection.  
  
## Exports  
  
| Export          | Description                                    |  
|-----------------|------------------------------------------------|  
| `Sqlite3::Error` | `code` (extended result code) and `message`; `isConstraint()` |  
  
## Constraint violations  
  
`isConstraint()` answers whether the error is one of the `SQLITE_CONSTRAINT`  
family (primary-key, unique, not-null, check, foreign-key). A service layer  
turns those into HTTP 409/422; every other code is a 500. The check is on  
the extended code's primary part (`code & 0xff`), so any specific  
constraint code the engine reports matches.

modules.name: std::sqlite3::statement
modules.doc:
# Statement  
  
`Sqlite3::Statement`, one compiled SQL statement. Wraps the `sqlite3_stmt*`  
that `Connection::prepare` produces, binds parameters, steps through rows  
and reads columns; finalizes on drop.  
  
## Exports  
  
| Export          | Description                                          |  
|-----------------|------------------------------------------------------|  
| `Sqlite3::Statement` | `bindNull`, `bindInt`, `bindReal`, `bindText`, `bindBlob`, `step`, `columnCount`, `columnIsNull`, `columnInt`, `columnReal`, `columnText`, `columnBlob`, `reset` |  
| `Sqlite3::Step` | `ROW` or `DONE`, what `step` reports                |  
  
## Binding and reading  
  
Parameter indexes are 1-based, the way SQLite itself counts them in the C  
API (`?1` is index 1). Column indexes are 0-based. `bindText` and  
`bindBlob` pass `SQLITE_TRANSIENT` to SQLite, so the bound bytes are  
copied at bind time and the caller's buffer can go away before `step`.  
`SQLITE_TRANSIENT` is SQLite's own documented sentinel — the  
`sqlite3_bind_text` docs define it as "a special destructor (...) which  
makes SQLite copy the bytes" — spelled here as the pointer value `-1`  
because the C header defines it as a cast of -1 to the destructor's  
function-pointer type.  
  
`step()` returns `Result::OK(Step::ROW)` for each row and  
`Result::OK(Step::DONE)` when the statement is finished; anything else is  
an `Sqlite3::Error`. Column getters coerce the value the way SQLite does  
(`columnInt` on a TEXT column parses a number); `columnIsNull` tells the  
two cases apart that a coercion would blur. After an error the statement  
is reset before reuse.  
  
## Reuse  
  
`reset()` rewinds the statement so it can run again with new bindings;  
rebinding replaces every bound parameter. The statement stays compiled, so  
a query run many times prepares once.

modules.name: std::sqlite3::transaction
modules.doc:
# Transaction  
  
`Sqlite3::Transaction`, the guard `Connection::begin` returns. `commit()`  
commits; dropping the transaction without `commit` rolls it back, so an  
early `return` or an error path cannot leave a transaction open.  
  
## Exports  
  
| Export               | Description                                |  
|----------------------|--------------------------------------------|  
| `Sqlite3::Transaction` | `commit`, `rollback`; rolls back on drop |  
  
## The Drop contract  
  
A `Transaction` that is dropped while still open runs `ROLLBACK` on its  
connection. Nothing can be reported at that point, so a rollback on drop  
is silent and best effort: if the connection is already closed, the  
rollback does nothing. Code that wants the outcome calls `commit` or  
`rollback` and gets a `Result`; drop is the safety net, not the API.  
  
After `commit` or `rollback`, calling either method again is a misuse  
error, not a panic. A failed `commit` leaves the transaction unfinished,  
so drop still cleans up.  
  
## Lifetime  
  
The transaction does not own its connection: it holds the address of the  
`Connection` that produced it and reads the connection's live handle on  
every use, so a transaction outliving a `close()` is refused with a misuse  
error instead of touching freed memory. What it cannot survive is the  
`Connection` value itself being gone — the same contract a `MutexGuard`  
has with its mutex, and declaration order gives it in ordinary use: the  
connection declared first drops last, after every transaction and  
statement it produced.

modules.name: std::string
modules.doc:
# String Module  
  
Owned, heap-backed UTF-8 byte string type and related utilities.  
  
## Overview  
  
`String` is a value-type record whose `data` buffer lives on the heap.  
It implements `Drop` so the buffer is freed automatically when the  
owning binding goes out of scope, and `Clone` for explicit deep copies.  
Its storage is an owned UTF-8 byte buffer with a byte-counted `len` field.  
  
`str` is the primitive immutable string-slice type (`const char*` in C).  
In v0.4 it remains a borrowed NUL-terminated UTF-8 byte view.  
String literals have type `str`. Use `String::create(s)` to create an  
owned copy from a `str`.  
  
Interior NUL bytes are preserved in owned storage.  
toStr() is a zero-copy interop view.  
C-string consumers may stop at the first interior NUL.  
  
## Memory Layout  
  
```text  
  String  
  ┌──────────────┐  
  │ data ────────┼──────► ┌───┬───┬───┬───┬───┬───┬───┬───┐  
  │ len: 5       │        │ h │ e │ l │ l │ o │   │   │   │  
  │ cap: 8       │        └───┴───┴───┴───┴───┴───┴───┴───┘  
  └──────────────┘        ◄── used bytes ──►◄─ reserved ──►  
```  
  
Fields mirror the C runtime's `IgnisString` layout exactly:  
- `data` — pointer to the backing byte buffer (or `null` before init)  
- `len`  — number of bytes currently stored  
- `cap`  — total bytes allocated  
  
## UTF-8 Scanning and Bytes  
  
`String` stays byte-backed. APIs that need parser or diagnostic offsets keep  
those byte positions internal to the caller while decoding `char` values at  
explicit byte boundaries.  
  
`charAt` and `pushChar` work with decoded `char` values, while `byteAt`,  
`pushByte`, `forEachByte`, `findByte`, `trimWhere`, and `split` keep raw byte  
behavior explicit.  
  
## Higher-Order Iteration Methods  
  
String provides callback-based operations for char/byte iteration,  
searching, trimming, and splitting:  
  
| Method        | Callback signature   | Returns            | Description                        |  
|---------------|----------------------|--------------------|------------------------------------|  
| `forEach`     | `(char) -> void`     | `void`             | Iterate scalar `char` values       |  
| `forEachByte` | `(u8) -> void`       | `void`             | Iterate over every byte            |  
| `map`         | `(char) -> char`     | `String`           | Transform scalar `char` values     |  
| `mapBytes`    | `(u8) -> u8`         | `String`           | Transform bytes directly           |  
| `findByte`    | `(u8) -> boolean`    | `Option<u64>`      | Index of first matching byte       |  
| `findLastByte`| `(u8) -> boolean`    | `Option<u64>`      | Index of last matching byte        |  
| `trimWhere`   | `(u8) -> boolean`    | `String`           | Strip leading/trailing bytes       |  
| `split`       | `(u8) -> boolean`    | `Vector<String>`   | Split into segments                |  
  
All callbacks are `@noescape`: the closure must not outlive the method call.  
  
## Byte Conversion  
  
| Method    | Returns         | Description                        |  
|-----------|-----------------|------------------------------------|  
| `toBytes` | `Vector<u8>`    | Copy bytes into a byte vector      |  
| `toChars` | `Vector<char>`  | Copy bytes into a char vector      |  
  
## Numeric Conversions  
  
`String::create` is overloaded for all numeric primitives (`i8` through  
`f64`), plus `str`. Extension methods provide `.toString()` on every  
primitive type.  
  
## Example  
  
```ignis  
import Io from "std::io";  
  
function main(): i32 {  
  let greeting: String = String::create("hello");  
  let world: str = " world";  
  let msg: String = greeting.concat(world);  
  
  Io::println(msg);  
  
  // Byte-level: trim whitespace and split on commas  
  let csv: String = String::create("  a,b,c  ");  
  let trimmed: String = csv.trimWhere((b: u8): boolean -> { return b == 32; });  
  let parts: Vector<String> = trimmed.split((b: u8): boolean -> { return b == 44; });  
  // parts: ["a", "b", "c"]  
  
  return 0;  
}  
```

modules.name: std::sync
modules.doc:
# Sync  
  
Synchronization building blocks.  
  
## Exports  
  
| Export          | Description                            |  
|-----------------|----------------------------------------|  
| `Ordering`      | Memory ordering of an atomic operation |  
| `AtomicBool`    | `boolean` updated atomically           |  
| `AtomicU32`     | `u32` updated atomically               |  
| `AtomicU64`     | `u64` updated atomically               |  
| `AtomicI64`     | `i64` updated atomically               |  
| `AtomicPtr<T>`  | `*mut T` updated atomically            |  
| `Mutex<T>`      | Value one thread at a time may access  |  
| `MutexGuard<T>` | A locked mutex; unlocks on drop        |  
| `Condvar`       | Sleep until another thread notifies    |  
| `Arc<T>`        | Shared ownership with an atomic count  |  
| `Shared<T>`     | `Arc<Mutex<T>>` under a shorter name   |  
| `Channel<T>`    | A new channel's first sender and receiver |  
| `Sender<T>`     | Sending end of a channel               |  
| `Receiver<T>`   | Receiving end of a channel             |  
| `ThreadPool`    | Fixed set of worker threads running jobs |  
  
See `std::sync::atomic` for the ordering rules and the `compareExchange`  
result shape, `std::sync::mutex` for locking and waiting, and  
`std::sync::arc` for shared ownership, `std::sync::channel` for passing  
values between threads, and `std::sync::pool` for the thread pool.  
  
`Shared<T>` is the alias for `Arc<Mutex<T>>`, the shape sharing one mutable  
value between threads spells at every call site; use it for that, and spell  
`Arc<Mutex<T>>` out when the code around it is lock- and guard-heavy enough  
that naming each half reads clearer.

modules.name: std::sync::arc
modules.doc:
# Arc  
  
Shared ownership across threads with an atomic reference count.  
  
`Arc<T>` keeps one heap allocation alive while any clone of it exists.  
`clone` adds a reference, dropping a clone removes one, and the last one  
drops the value and frees the allocation. The count is atomic, so clones  
can move to and drop on different threads.  
  
`get` gives only shared access: several threads may read the value at once.  
To mutate it, share a `Mutex` or an atomic (`Shared<T>`, the alias for  
`Arc<Mutex<T>>`).  
  
## Thread safety  
  
`Arc<T>` requires `T: Send & Sync`: a clone on another thread reads the same  
value (Sync), and whichever thread drops the last clone drops the value  
(Send). `Arc<Rc<i32>>` is rejected. The allocation is reached through a raw  
pointer, so `Arc` declares `Send` and `Sync` itself.  
  
## Layout  
  
```text  
  ┌──────────────┬─────────────┬──────────────┐  
  │ strong (u64) │ padding     │ T payload    │  
  └──────────────┴─────────────┴──────────────┘  
  ^ block                      ^ block + headerSize(alignOf<T>)  
```  
  
## Example  
  
```ignis  
import Arc from "std::sync";  
  
function main(): i32 {  
  let first: Arc<i32> = Arc::new<i32>(42);  
  let second: Arc<i32> = first.clone();  
  
  return *second.get();  
}  
```

modules.name: std::sync::atomic
modules.doc:
# Atomics  
  
Atomic integers, booleans and pointers built on the compiler's atomic  
primitives (`@atomicLoad`, `@atomicStore`, `@atomicRmw`,  
`@atomicCompareExchange`).  
  
## Overview  
  
Every type wraps one value and changes it only through `&self`, so a shared  
reference is enough to update it from several threads. The methods take the  
memory ordering as a runtime `Ordering` and map it to the literal ordering the  
primitive needs.  
  
| Type           | Value      | Integer operations |  
|----------------|------------|--------------------|  
| `AtomicBool`   | `boolean`  | no                 |  
| `AtomicU32`    | `u32`      | yes                |  
| `AtomicU64`    | `u64`      | yes                |  
| `AtomicI64`    | `i64`      | yes                |  
| `AtomicPtr<T>` | `*mut T`   | no                 |  
  
## Orderings  
  
| Operation                  | Accepted orderings                   |  
|----------------------------|--------------------------------------|  
| `load`                     | `RELAXED`, `ACQUIRE`, `SEQ_CST`      |  
| `store`                    | `RELAXED`, `RELEASE`, `SEQ_CST`      |  
| `swap`, `fetch*`           | any                                  |  
| `compareExchange` success  | any                                  |  
| `compareExchange` failure  | `RELAXED`, `ACQUIRE`, `SEQ_CST`      |  
  
Any other ordering panics with a message naming the operation and the  
ordering. It is never clamped: a load that asks for `RELEASE` is a logic  
error, and silently weakening or strengthening it would hide that.  
  
Two `compareExchange` pairs run stronger than written, because GCC rejects a  
failure ordering stronger than the success one: a `SEQ_CST` failure runs the  
success ordering as `SEQ_CST` too, and `(RELAXED, ACQUIRE)` runs as  
`(ACQUIRE, ACQUIRE)`. Every other valid pair, including `(RELEASE, ACQUIRE)`,  
runs as written.  
  
## Compare-exchange  
  
`compareExchange(expected, desired, success, failure)` is strong: it never  
fails spuriously. It returns `Result::OK(previous)` when it wrote `desired`  
(`previous` equals `expected`) and `Result::ERROR(observed)` with the value  
it found otherwise.  
  
## Example  
  
```ignis  
import AtomicU64, Ordering from "std::sync";  
  
function main(): i32 {  
  let counter: AtomicU64 = AtomicU64::new(0);  
  counter.fetchAdd(1, Ordering::RELAXED);  
  
  return counter.load(Ordering::SEQ_CST) as i32;  
}  
```  
  
## Arithmetic  
  
`fetchAdd` and `fetchSub` wrap on overflow. Every `fetch*` and `swap`  
returns the value held before the operation.

modules.name: std::sync::channel
modules.doc:
# Channel  
  
An unbounded many-producer, many-consumer queue between threads.  
  
## Exports  
  
| Export        | Description                                         |  
|---------------|-----------------------------------------------------|  
| `Channel<T>`  | `new` creates a channel; holds its two first ends   |  
| `Sender<T>`   | Puts values in the channel; cloneable and Send      |  
| `Receiver<T>` | Takes values out of the channel; cloneable and Send |  
  
## Sending and receiving  
  
`Channel::new<T>()` returns a `Channel<T>` whose `sender` and `receiver`  
fields are the first two ends; move them out into their own bindings.  
Values come out in the order they went in. Every end can be cloned, and  
the clones can move to other threads, so any number of threads may send  
and receive. Each value is received exactly once, by one receiver.  
  
- `send(value)` never blocks. It returns `Result::ERROR(value)`, giving the  
  value back, once every receiver is gone.  
- `recv()` blocks until a value arrives and returns `Option::SOME(value)`.  
  Once every sender is gone and the queue is empty it returns  
  `Option::NONE`, so a receiving loop ends when the producers do.  
- `tryRecv()` returns `Option::NONE` instead of blocking when the queue is  
  empty.  
  
## Ownership  
  
The ends share one heap block. The queue and the counts of live senders  
and receivers sit behind one `Mutex`, and one `Condvar` wakes blocked  
receivers. The end that brings both counts to zero, under the lock, drops  
the block: the values still in the queue are dropped with it.  
  
## Thread safety  
  
`T` has to be Send: a value moves from the sending thread to the receiving  
one. It does not have to be Sync, because no thread ever holds a reference  
to a queued value. That is also why the block is not an `Arc`, which would  
require `T: Sync`. The ends hold a raw pointer to the block, so they  
declare `Send` themselves.  
  
## Example  
  
```ignis  
import Channel, Receiver, Sender from "std::sync";  
import JoinHandle, Thread from "std::thread";  
  
function main(): i32 {  
  let channel: Channel<i32> = Channel::new<i32>();  
  let sender: Sender<i32> = channel.sender;  
  let receiver: Receiver<i32> = channel.receiver;  
  let producer: JoinHandle<void> = Thread::spawn<void>((): void -> {  
      (@move sender).send(42);  
    });  
  
  producer.join();  
  
  return receiver.recv().unwrapOr(0);  
}  
```

modules.name: std::sync::mutex
modules.doc:
# Mutex and Condvar  
  
Mutual exclusion and condition variables on top of POSIX threads.  
  
## Exports  
  
| Export          | Description                                          |  
|-----------------|------------------------------------------------------|  
| `Mutex<T>`      | Owns a `T` that one thread at a time may access      |  
| `MutexGuard<T>` | Proof that the mutex is locked; unlocks on drop      |  
| `Condvar`       | Lets a thread sleep until another one notifies it    |  
  
## Locking  
  
`lock` blocks until the calling thread owns the mutex and returns a guard;  
`tryLock` returns `Option::NONE` instead of blocking when another thread  
holds it. The guard reaches the value with `read` and `get`, and dropping  
the guard unlocks the mutex. Locking a mutex again on the thread that holds  
it deadlocks, as a default POSIX mutex does.  
  
A guard has to be dropped on the thread that locked the mutex. It holds raw  
pointers, so it is not Send and cannot be moved into a spawned task.  
  
## Thread safety  
  
`Mutex<T>` requires `T: Send` and declares Send and Sync: the lock lets one  
thread at a time reach the value, so a mutex is Send and Sync whenever `T`  
is Send, even when `T` is not Sync. To share a mutex between threads, put it  
in an `Arc` (`Shared<T>`, the alias for `Arc<Mutex<T>>`).  
  
## Waiting  
  
`Condvar::wait(&mut guard)` atomically unlocks the guard's mutex and sleeps  
until a notification, then locks it again before returning. Wakeups can be  
spurious, so wait in a loop that re-checks the condition.  
  
## Errors  
  
Every POSIX call's return code is checked. `lock`, `new` and `wait` panic  
with the function's name when it fails. An unlock, a notification or a  
destruction that fails panics with a message that starts with `std::sync:`:  
it means the lock was misused, for example a `Mutex` dropped while a guard  
still holds it, or a `Condvar` dropped while a thread waits on it.  
  
## Host assumptions  
  
The `pthread_mutex_t` and `pthread_cond_t` are stored inline, in `u64`  
arrays sized for Linux x86-64 glibc: 40 bytes for a mutex and 48 bytes for a  
condition variable, both 8-byte aligned. Another target needs its own sizes.  
  
An initialized glibc mutex or condition variable holds no pointer to  
itself, so moving one that nobody is using is safe there. A `Mutex` must not  
move while a guard is alive, and a `Condvar` must not move while a thread  
waits on it: the guard and the waiter hold their addresses. Keeping them in  
an `Arc`, or in a local that stays put, satisfies both.  
  
## Example  
  
```ignis  
import Mutex, MutexGuard from "std::sync";  
  
function main(): i32 {  
  let mutex: Mutex<i32> = Mutex::new<i32>(41);  
  let mut guard: MutexGuard<i32> = mutex.lock();  
  let value: &mut i32 = guard.get();  
  
  *value += 1;  
  
  return *guard.read();  
}  
```

modules.doc:
# Terminal Module  
  
Semantic terminal helpers for ANSI-capable command-line applications.  
  
## Purpose  
  
Use this module when a program needs **readable terminal intent** instead of  
manually assembling ANSI fragments.  
  
The public API answers questions like:  
- "How do I render text in red and then reset the terminal?"  
- "How do I clear the screen or move the cursor?"  
- "How do I avoid styling output when stdout is not a terminal?"  
  
The module intentionally does **not** expose raw ANSI assembly as the primary  
contract. Callers work with `Terminal::Style`, `Terminal::Screen`, and  
`Terminal::Cursor`, while private helpers translate those semantic requests  
into escape sequences.  
  
## Quick path  
  
1. Build a style with `Terminal::Style::new()`.  
2. Apply colors and attributes.  
3. Call `apply(text)` or use `colorText` / `styledText`.  
4. Check `isOutputTerminal()` before styling if plain output is required for  
   redirected streams.  
  
## Public surface  
  
| Area | API | Use when |  
|------|-----|----------|  
| Text styling | `Terminal::Style`, `colorText`, `styledText`, `reset` | You want semantic color/attribute output with automatic trailing reset |  
| Screen control | `Terminal::Screen::clear`, `clearLine` | You need simple full-screen or line clearing |  
| Cursor control | `Terminal::Cursor::{moveTo, save, restore, hide, show}` | You need TUI-style cursor positioning or visibility control |  
| Capability checks | `isInputTerminal`, `isOutputTerminal`, `isErrorTerminal` | You need to branch on whether a file descriptor is a terminal |  
| Window size | `outputSize`, `errorSize` | You need to fit a line to the terminal's width |  
  
## Design boundary  
  
```text  
  Caller intent  
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  
  │ Terminal::Style::new().foreground(...).apply(text)  │  
  │ Terminal::Screen::clear()                           │  
  │ Terminal::Cursor::moveTo(row, column)               │  
  └──────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────┘  
                             │ semantic API  
                             ▼  
  Private implementation  
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  
  │ ansiSgr(code)                                        │  
  │ ansiCsi(command)                                    │  
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  
```  
  
This split is deliberate:  
- Public code stays easy to read and review.  
- Escape-sequence details stay centralized.  
- Tests can assert high-level behavior without calling low-level helpers.  
  
## Behavior notes  
  
- Styled helpers append a trailing reset automatically.  
- Cursor coordinates are **one-based**, matching common ANSI terminal usage.  
- Capability checks currently rely on `isatty` through `std::libc` and are  
  therefore limited to the supported POSIX-style hosts enabled by the  
  `@configFlag` annotations.  
- This module does not implement raw mode, alternate screen buffers, event  
  input, or terminal layout/widgets.  
  
## Example  
  
```ignis  
import Terminal from "std::terminal";  
  
function main(): i32 {  
  if (Terminal::isOutputTerminal()) {  
    let mut style: Terminal::Style = Terminal::Style::new();  
    style.foreground(Terminal::TerminalColor::GREEN);  
    style.attribute(Terminal::TerminalAttribute::BOLD);  
  }  
  
  let heading: String = Terminal::colorText("ready", Terminal::TerminalColor::GREEN);  
  let clear: String = Terminal::Screen::clear();  
  let moveHome: String = Terminal::Cursor::moveTo(1, 1);  
  return 0;  
}  
```

modules.doc:
# Text  
  
Position conversion between UTF-8 byte offsets and editor positions.  
  
## Overview  
  
Compiler spans are UTF-8 byte offsets into a source text. Editors that  
speak the Language Server Protocol address the same text as a 0-based line  
plus a 0-based column counted in UTF-16 code units, the protocol's default  
position encoding. `Text::LineIndex` converts in both directions.  
  
```text  
  source: "a😀b\n"          bytes: a=0  😀=1..5  b=5  \n=6  
  
  byte offset 5  ── position ──▶  line 0, character 3   (a=1, 😀=2)  
  line 0, character 3  ── offset ──▶  byte offset 5  
```  
  
## APIs  
  
| Function                          | Description                                  |  
|-----------------------------------|----------------------------------------------|  
| `Text::LineIndex::create`         | Index a source text (takes ownership)        |  
| `Text::LineIndex::position`       | Byte offset to line and UTF-16 column        |  
| `Text::LineIndex::offset`         | Line and UTF-16 column to byte offset        |  
| `Text::LineIndex::endPosition`    | Position of the end of the text              |  
| `Text::LineIndex::lineCount`      | Number of lines (a trailing `\n` opens one)  |  
| `Text::utf16Length`               | UTF-16 code units of the whole text          |  
  
## Semantics  
  
The rules mirror the host language server (`crates/ignis_lsp/src/convert.rs`):  
  
- Only `\n` starts a new line. In CRLF text the `\r` is the last column of  
  its line, so the offset just before `\n` has a column one past the text.  
- A character outside the Basic Multilingual Plane (4 UTF-8 bytes) counts as  
  two UTF-16 units, every other character as one.  
- `position` of an offset inside a multi-byte character reports the column  
  of that character's first byte. An offset past the end reports the end.  
- `offset` of a column past the end of a line walks through the line break  
  and lands on the start of the next line. A column that falls inside a  
  surrogate pair lands after the character. A line past the last one  
  returns the text length.  
- The host only indexes valid UTF-8. Here, a byte that does not start a  
  complete, well-formed sequence counts as one character of one byte and one  
  UTF-16 unit, the width of the U+FFFD replacement character.  
  
## Example  
  
```ignis  
import Text from "std::text";  
  
function main(): i32 {  
  let index: Text::LineIndex = Text::LineIndex::create(String::create("hola\nmundo\n"));  
  
  let position: Text::Position = index.position(7);  
  // position.line == 1, position.character == 2  
  
  let offset: u64 = index.offset(Text::Position { line: 1, character: 2 });  
  // offset == 7  
  return 0;  
}  
```

modules.name: std::thread
modules.doc:
# Thread  
  
Operating system threads on top of POSIX threads.  
  
## Exports  
  
| Export          | Description                                         |  
|-----------------|-----------------------------------------------------|  
| `Thread`        | `spawn` a task on a new thread, `currentId`         |  
| `JoinHandle<T>` | Owns a running thread; `join` waits for its result  |  
  
## Spawning and joining  
  
`Thread::spawn<T>(task)` runs `task` on a new thread and returns a  
`JoinHandle<T>`. `join()` waits for the thread to finish and returns what the  
task returned. The task parameter is `@sendable`, so the compiler checks at  
every call that whatever the closure captures can move to another thread.  
The result moves from the spawned thread to the joining one, so `T` has to  
be Send.  
`join` takes `self`: it consumes the handle, so a handle is joined at most  
once and using it after `join` is a use-after-move compile error.  
  
A task with nothing to report returns `void`: `Thread::spawn<void>` gives a  
`JoinHandle<void>` whose `join` only waits.  
  
Dropping a handle without joining it detaches the thread: it keeps running,  
nothing waits for it, and its result is dropped when it finishes. A detached  
thread that is still running when `main` returns is ended with the process,  
together with whatever it still owns, so its control block and anything it  
has not dropped yet are never freed. Join every thread whose cleanup has to  
finish before the program ends.  
  
## Panics  
  
A panic in a spawned thread ends the whole process with exit code 101, the  
same as a panic on the main thread. There is no unwinding and `join` never  
observes a panicked thread.  
  
## Ownership of a spawned thread  
  
`spawn` allocates one control block shared by the handle and the thread. It  
holds a reference count that starts at 2, the boxed task, and a heap slot for  
the result:  
  
- The thread runs the task, writes the result into the slot, and drops its  
  reference.  
- `join` waits for the thread, moves the result out of the slot and marks the  
  block joined. The consumed handle drops its reference when `join` returns.  
- Dropping an unjoined handle detaches the thread and drops its reference.  
  
Whichever side drops the last reference drops the result still in the slot  
(only when nobody joined), frees the slot, the task's closures and the block.  
Every release happens after the task ran, so an unjoined slot always holds a  
result. The count is atomic, so the block is freed exactly once.  
  
## Host assumptions  
  
`pthread_t` is bound as `u64`, which is its definition on Linux (glibc and  
musl) for 64-bit targets. A target whose `pthread_t` is not a 64-bit integer  
needs its own binding.  
  
## Example  
  
```ignis  
import JoinHandle, Thread from "std::thread";  
  
function main(): i32 {  
  let handle: JoinHandle<i32> = Thread::spawn<i32>((): i32 -> 6 * 7);  
  
  return handle.join();  
}  
```

modules.name: std::toml
modules.doc:
# TOML  
  
TOML parsing, lookup, and serialization front-end for Ignis data.  
  
## Overview  
  
The `Toml` namespace parses UTF-8 TOML text into owned tables, arrays, and  
values. It also exposes writer helpers backed by `std::serializer` for  
serializing primitive and `Serialize` values as TOML-compatible output.  
  
## Types  
  
| Type             | Description                                      |  
|------------------|--------------------------------------------------|  
| `TomlDocument`   | Root document with table storage                 |  
| `TomlTable`      | Key/value table                                  |  
| `TomlArray`      | Ordered TOML array values                        |  
| `TomlValue`      | Tagged TOML scalar, array, or table value        |  
| `TomlError`      | Structured parse or lookup error with span       |  
  
## APIs  
  
| Function            | Description                                      |  
|---------------------|--------------------------------------------------|  
| `Toml::parse`       | Parse TOML text into a `TomlDocument`            |  
| `Toml::writer`      | TOML writer configuration                        |  
| `Toml::writeRoot`   | Serialize a root `Serialize` value               |  
  
## Notes  
  
TOML root output must be a record-like serialized value. Scalar roots are  
rejected by the shared serializer because they are not valid TOML documents.  
A record nested in the root is written as an inline table on its field's  
line (`owner = { name = "Ada", age = 36 }`), recursively, and parses back  
with `Toml::parse`.  
  
## Example  
  
```ignis  
import Toml, TomlDocument, TomlError from "std::toml";  
  
function main(): i32 {  
  let parsed: Result<TomlDocument, TomlError> = Toml::parse("name = \"ignis\"\n");  
  return parsed.isOk() ? 0 : 1;  
}  
```

modules.name: std::toml::error
modules.doc:
# TOML Errors  
  
Structured TOML parse and lookup failures with source spans.  
  
## Overview  
  
`TomlError` pairs an error kind with a human-readable message and the byte  
span where the parser or lookup operation detected the problem. Lookup errors  
use the same type so callers can handle parse and access failures uniformly.  
  
## Error Flow  
  
```text  
  lexer/parser/lookup detects failure  
                │  
                ▼  
  TomlErrorKind + message + TomlSpan  
                │  
                ▼  
  Result::ERROR(TomlError)  
```  
  
Parse errors use spans from the original input. Lookup errors use the span of  
the missing path's nearest known location or the value that caused a type  
mismatch.

modules.name: std::toml::parser
modules.doc:
# TOML Parser  
  
Recursive-descent parser for tokenized TOML documents.  
  
## Overview  
  
This module consumes `TomlToken` streams and builds owned `TomlDocument`  
values. It handles table headers, arrays of tables, dotted keys, inline  
tables, arrays, scalar literals, and duplicate-key validation.

modules.name: std::toml::token
modules.doc:
# TOML Tokens  
  
Token and span types shared by the TOML lexer and parser.  
  
## Overview  
  
`TomlSpan` stores byte offsets into the original UTF-8 input. `TomlToken`  
owns its lexeme text so token streams remain valid after lexing completes.  
  
## Token Stream Shape  
  
The lexer emits structural punctuation, scalar literals, newlines, and a  
terminal `EOF` token. The parser consumes newline tokens explicitly because  
TOML uses line boundaries to terminate assignments and table headers.  
  
| Token group       | Kinds                                      |  
|-------------------|--------------------------------------------|  
| Punctuation       | brackets, braces, dot, equals, comma       |  
| Whitespace marker | `NEWLINE`                                  |  
| Key/value text    | `IDENTIFIER`, `STRING`                     |  
| Scalar literals   | `INTEGER`, `FLOAT`, `DATE_TIME`, `BOOLEAN` |  
| End marker        | `EOF`                                      |

modules.name: std::toml::value
modules.doc:
# TOML Values  
  
Owned TOML document, table, array, and scalar value model.  
  
## Overview  
  
The value layer stores parsed TOML data in owned Ignis records and provides  
lookup helpers for dotted paths. Tables preserve explicit table state so the  
parser can distinguish duplicate keys, table conflicts, and arrays of tables.

modules.name: std::types
modules.doc:
# Types Module  
  
Core runtime type identifiers.  
  
## Contents  
  
`Type::TypeId` provides compile-time constants that mirror the runtime's  
internal type tags. These are useful for diagnostics, FFI integrations,  
and low-level tooling that needs stable numeric identifiers for primitive  
types.  
  
| Constant  | Ignis Type |  
|-----------|------------|  
| `I8`      | `i8`       |  
| `I16`     | `i16`      |  
| `I32`     | `i32`      |  
| `I64`     | `i64`      |  
| `U8`      | `u8`       |  
| `U16`     | `u16`      |  
| `U32`     | `u32`      |  
| `U64`     | `u64`      |  
| `F32`     | `f32`      |  
| `F64`     | `f64`      |  
| `BOOL`    | `boolean`  |  
| `CHAR`    | `char`     |  
| `STRING`  | `str`      |  
| `POINTER` | `*T`       |  
  
For sum types, use dedicated modules:  
- `std::option` for `Option<S>`  
- `std::result` for `Result<T, E>`  
  
## Example  
  
```ignis  
  
function main(): i32 {  
  let id: u32 = Type::TypeId::I32;  
  return id as i32;  
}  
```

modules.name: std::vector
modules.doc:
# Vector Module  
  
Growable contiguous array backed by `std::memory`.  
  
## Overview  
  
`Vector<T>` stores elements in a contiguous heap allocation and grows  
capacity geometrically (`x2`) when needed.  
  
- `length` is the number of initialized elements  
- `capacity` is the number of elements that can be stored without reallocating  
- `data` points to the first element (or `null` when empty)  
  
## Memory Layout  
  
```text  
  Vector<T>  
  ┌──────────────┐  
  │ data ────────┼──────► ┌───┬───┬───┬───┬───┬───┬───┬───┐  
  │ length: 5    │        │ 0 │ 1 │ 2 │ 3 │ 4 │   │   │   │  
  │ capacity: 8  │        └───┴───┴───┴───┴───┴───┴───┴───┘  
  └──────────────┘        ◄── initialized ──►◄─ reserved ─►  
```  
  
## Growth Strategy  
  
When `push()` is called and `length == capacity`, the vector doubles its  
backing storage (or allocates 1 slot if currently empty):  
  
```text  
  push() when length == capacity  
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  
  │ old capacity = N                                                     │  
  │ new capacity = max(1, N * 2)                                         │  
  │ reallocate buffer to new capacity                                    │  
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  
  
  Example:  
    cap=0 → push → cap=1  
    cap=1 → push → cap=2  
    cap=2 → push → cap=4  
    cap=4 → push → cap=8  
```  
  
## Higher-Order Methods  
  
Vector provides callback-based operations for functional-style iteration,  
filtering, transformation, and aggregation:  
  
| Method       | Signature                                     | Description                           |  
|------------- |-----------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------|  
| `forEach`    | `(&T) -> void`                                | Iterate elements by immutable ref     |  
| `forEachMut` | `(&mut T) -> void`                            | Iterate elements by mutable ref       |  
| `filter`     | `(&T) -> boolean` → `Vector<T>`               | Keep matching elements                |  
| `any`        | `(&T) -> boolean` → `boolean`                 | Short-circuit existential check       |  
| `all`        | `(&T) -> boolean` → `boolean`                 | Short-circuit universal check         |  
| `findIndex`  | `(&T) -> boolean` → `Option<u64>`             | Index of first match                  |  
| `count`      | `(&T) -> boolean` → `u64`                     | Count matching elements               |  
| `reduce`     | `(T, &T) -> T` → `Option<T>`                 | Fold without initial value            |  
| `sort`       | `(&T, &T) -> i32`                             | In-place insertion sort               |  
| `map<U>`     | `(&T) -> U` → `Vector<U>`                    | Transform each element                |  
| `fold<U>`    | `U, (U, &T) -> U` → `U`                      | Fold with initial value               |  
  
All callbacks are `@noescape`: the closure must not outlive the method call.  
  
## Safety Notes  
  
This container performs manual memory management and raw pointer writes.  
It does not run element destructors automatically.  
  
The vector implements `Drop` and will automatically release its backing  
storage when it goes out of scope.  
  
## Example  
  
```ignis  
import Io from "std::io";  
  
function main(): i32 {  
  let mut values: Vector<i32> = Vector::new<i32>();  
  values.push(10);  
  values.push(20);  
  values.push(30);  
  
  // Functional-style: double every even element, then sum  
  let sum: i32 = values  
    .filter((x: &i32): boolean -> { return *x % 2 == 0; })  
    .map<i32>((x: &i32): i32 -> { return *x * 2; })  
    .fold<i32>(0, (acc: i32, x: &i32): i32 -> { return acc + *x; });  
  
  // Vector is automatically dropped here  
  return 0;  
}  
```

items.name: Char
items.doc:
Character and UTF-8 scalar classification helpers.  
  
Methods whose names include `Ascii` intentionally classify only ASCII  
characters. Methods without that prefix operate on native Unicode scalar  
`char` values.

items.name: asciiDigitValue
items.doc:
Returns the numeric value of an ASCII decimal digit.  
  
Non-ASCII digits, including Unicode decimal digits, return `Option::NONE`.

items.name: isAlpha

Returns whether `value` is an alphabetic Unicode scalar.  
  
This is an alias for `isAlpha` using the longer Rust-style name.  
  
# Example  
  
```ignis  
import Char from "std::char";  
  
let lambda: char = 'λ';  
  
lambda.isAlphabetic(); // true  
```

This is an alias for `isNumeric`.  
  
# Example  
  
```ignis

let digit: char = '9';  
  
digit.isDigit(); // true
```

Returns whether `value` is a hexadecimal ASCII scalar.  
  
This intentionally follows ASCII hexadecimal syntax. Use `isNumeric` for  
broader Unicode digit classification.  
  
# Example  
  
```ignis  
import Char from "std::char";  
  
let hex: char = 'F';  
let fullWidth: char = 'Ｇ';  
  
hex.isHexDigit();       // true  
fullWidth.isHexDigit(); // false  
```

should prefer the semantic classification helpers below.

Cli
items.doc:
CLI parsing and help-generation utilities.  
  
The namespace exposes a bounded public surface centered on:  
- `Command` for spec definition and parsing  
- `Matches` for query access  
- `CliError` for stable failures

items.name: CliError
items.doc:
A parsing or validation error.  
  
The current bounded parser uses a single message field so callers can show  
stable human-readable output without depending on backend diagnostics.

members.name: message
members.doc: Stable error text suitable for user-facing CLI messages.

members.name: clone
members.doc:
Returns an owned copy of the error.  
  
# Example  
  
```ignis  
let duplicate: Cli::CliError = error.clone();  
```

items.name: Command
items.doc:
Builder for bounded command-line parsers.  
  
`Command` owns a declared option specification and can parse either an  
explicit argv vector or the current process argv.

members.name: name
members.doc: Canonical command name used for help rendering and argv fallback.

members.name: about
members.doc: Optional one-line about text shown in help output.

members.name: specs
members.doc: Declared flag and option specifications in stable insertion order.

members.name: new
members.doc:
Creates a new empty command specification.  
  
# Arguments  
  
- `name`: command/program name to display in help output.  
  
# Example  
  
```ignis  
let command: Cli::Command = Cli::Command::new("tool");  
```

members.name: aboutText
members.doc:
Sets the one-line about text used by `renderHelp()`.  
  
# Example  
  
```ignis  
command.aboutText("Build project artifacts.");  
```

members.name: appendSpecHelp
members.doc:
Appends one formatted help line for a declared option spec.  
  
The output format is intentionally compact and deterministic so tests and  
CLI callers can rely on stable rendering.  
  
# Example  
  
```ignis  
command.appendSpecHelp(&mut help, spec);  
```

members.name: findSpec
members.doc:
Finds the declared spec matching a long name or short alias.  
  
# Example  
  
```ignis  
let spec: Option<&Cli::OptionSpec> = command.findSpec(&String::create("verbose"));  
```

members.name: flag
members.signature: flag(&mut self, longName: str, shortName: str, help: str): void
members.doc:
Declares a boolean flag.  
  
# Arguments  
  
- `longName`: canonical long name without `--`  
- `shortName`: optional short alias without `-`  
- `help`: help text shown in deterministic help output  
  
# Example  
  
```ignis  
command.flag("verbose", "v", "Enable verbose output.");  
```

members.name: option
members.signature: option(&mut self, longName: str, shortName: str, help: str): void
members.doc:
Declares an option that consumes the next argv item as its value.  
  
# Example  
  
```ignis  
command.option("output", "o", "Write output file.");  
```

members.name: parse
members.doc:
Parses an explicit argv vector.  
  
# Arguments  
  
- `args`: argv-style vector where index `0` is the program name.  
  
# Supported behavior  
  
- long flags and valued options  
- short flags and valued options  
- ordered positionals  
- `--` terminator  
  
# Unsupported behavior  
  
- grouped short flags  
- `--opt=value`  
- repeated-value aggregation helpers  
- default values and env fallbacks  
  
# Example  
  
```ignis  
let mut args: Vector<String> = Vector::new<String>();  
args.push(String::create("tool"));  
args.push(String::create("--verbose"));  
let result: Result<Cli::Matches, Cli::CliError> = command.parse(&args);  
```

members.name: parseOption
members.signature: parseOption(&self, options: &mut Vector<OptionValue>, name: &String, token: &String, args: &Vector<String>, index: u64): Result<u64, CliError>
members.doc:
Parses one long or short option token and advances the argv index.  
  
# Arguments  
  
- `options`: output vector that accumulates parsed option occurrences  
- `name`: canonicalized token text without `-`/`--`  
- `token`: original raw token for stable error reporting  
- `args`: full argv vector  
- `index`: current token index within `args`  
  
# Returns  
  
- `Result::OK(nextIndex)` when parsing succeeds  
- `Result::ERROR(CliError)` when the option is undeclared or missing a required value  
  
# Example  
  
```ignis  
let nextIndex: Result<u64, Cli::CliError> = command.parseOption(&mut options, &name, token, &args, 1);  
```

members.name: parseProcess
members.doc:
Parses the current process argv.  
  
# Returns  
  
The same result shape as `parse(&args)`, but using owned argv copies from  
`Process::args()`.  
  
# Example  
  
```ignis  
let result: Result<Cli::Matches, Cli::CliError> = command.parseProcess();  
```

members.name: programName
members.doc:
Resolves the program name from argv or falls back to the command name.  
  
# Example  
  
```ignis  
let program: String = command.programName(&args);  
```

members.name: renderHelp
members.doc:
Renders deterministic help text from the command specification.  
  
# Output order  
  
1. usage line  
2. blank line + about text when present  
3. blank line + options section when at least one spec exists  
4. options in declaration order  
  
# Example  
  
```ignis  
let help: String = command.renderHelp();  
```

items.name: Matches
items.doc:
Parsed command-line matches.  
  
`Matches` stores owned data so callers can inspect results without  
borrowing from the original argv vector.

members.name: program
members.doc: Program name taken from `argv[0]` or the command name fallback.

members.name: options
members.doc: Parsed flag/option occurrences in arrival order.

members.name: positionals
members.doc: Parsed positional arguments after option handling.

members.name: find
members.doc:
Finds the first stored option occurrence by canonical long name.  
  
This helper is private because the public API should expose semantic  
queries such as `has()` and `value()` instead of raw storage traversal.  
  
# Example  
  
```ignis  
let entry: Option<&Cli::OptionValue> = matches.find("output");  
```

members.name: has
members.doc:
Returns `true` when the named flag or option was present.  
  
# Arguments  
  
- `name`: canonical long option name.  
  
# Example  
  
```ignis  
let verboseEnabled: boolean = matches.has("verbose");  
```

members.name: positional
members.doc:
Returns the positional argument at `index`.  
  
Positionals remain ordered exactly as parsed, including tokens that  
appeared after `--`.  
  
# Example  
  
```ignis  
let firstArg: Option<String> = matches.positional(0);  
```

members.name: programName
members.doc:
Returns an owned copy of the resolved program name.  
  
# Example  
  
```ignis  
let name: String = matches.programName();  
```

members.name: value
members.doc:
Returns the first stored value for a named option.  
  
# Returns  
  
- `Option::SOME(String)` when the named option was present with a value  
- `Option::NONE` when the option is absent or is a boolean flag  
  
# Example  
  
```ignis  
let output: Option<String> = matches.value("output");  
```

Option definition used by `Command`.  
  
This record describes one accepted long/short option pair.

members.name: shortName

One parsed option or flag occurrence.  
  
`OptionValue` is an internal storage shape used by `Matches`. Boolean  
flags set `hasValue = false` and store an empty `value` string.

items.name: cliStringAfterPrefix
items.doc:
Returns the substring after a known prefix length.  
  
# Arguments  
  
- `value`: source token.  
- `prefixLength`: number of leading bytes to skip.  
  
# Returns  
  
A new owned `String` containing the suffix.  
  
# Example  
  
```ignis  
let suffix: String = cliStringAfterPrefix(&String::create("--output"), 2);  
// suffix == "output"  
```

items.name: cliStringEquals
items.doc:
Returns whether an owned string equals a `str` literal.  
  
This is a private parser helper that keeps equality checks readable in the  
argv scan loop.  
  
# Example  
  
```ignis  
let same: boolean = cliStringEquals(&String::create("--help"), "--help");  
```

items.name: cliStringStartsWith
items.doc:
Returns whether `value` begins with `prefix`.  
  
# Notes  
  
- This check is byte-oriented.  
- It allocates a temporary owned `String` for the prefix comparison.  
  
# Example  
  
```ignis  
let isLong: boolean = cliStringStartsWith(&String::create("--verbose"), "--");  
```

Dense deterministic set for `u32` bit indexes.  
  
`BitSet` stores membership in little-endian `u64` words. It is intended for  
compiler-style dataflow and membership sets where ids are dense enough that a  
bit-vector is simpler than a hash table.

items.name: HashMap
items.doc:
Deterministic open-addressed map from `K` to `V`.  
  
This container owns both keys and values. Replacing or removing an entry  
drops the previous key/value exactly once.  
  
Declared `Send` and `Sync` although it holds a raw pointer: the map  
owns its heap buffers exclusively, so moving it moves the only handle to the  
buffers, and a shared reference only reads it. An instance is  
Send or Sync only when `K` and `V` are.

logical entries at the current load-factor policy.  
  
# Example  
  
```ignis  
import HashMap from "std::collections";  
  
let map: HashMap<i32, i32> = HashMap::new<i32, i32>(64);  
```

items.name: Env
items.doc:
Process environment accessors.  
  
Functions in this namespace read and mutate the current process environment  
through the host C runtime. Read APIs return owned Ignis values so callers do  
not borrow from host-managed environment storage.

items.name: EnvError
items.doc:
Error returned when a required environment variable is missing.  
  
`EnvError` preserves the requested variable name so callers can report a  
precise configuration failure without separately storing the lookup key.

members.name: name
members.doc: Environment variable name that was requested.

items.name: currentDir
items.doc:
Returns the current working directory as an owned path.  
  
The path is copied from `getcwd(3)` into a `Path::PathBuf`. The returned  
value is absolute on supported POSIX hosts and does not borrow from the  
temporary C buffer used for the syscall.  
  
# Returns  
  
- `Result::OK(path)` when the host current directory can be read.  
- `Result::ERROR(error)` with the captured `errno` when `getcwd` fails.

items.name: get
has
items.doc:
Returns `true` when the environment variable is present.  
  
Presence is independent from value length. A variable set to the empty  
string is still present and therefore returns `true`.  
  
# Arguments  
  
- `name`: environment variable name to check.  
  
# Returns  
  
`true` when the host environment contains `name`, otherwise `false`.  
  
# When To Use  
  
Use `has` when presence matters but the actual value does not. Use `get`  
or `var` when the value must be read. `has` still calls into the host  
environment; it is not a cached result.  
  
# Example  
  
```ignis  
import Env from "std::env";  
  
Env::set("IGNIS_EMPTY", "");  
let exists: boolean = Env::has("IGNIS_EMPTY"); // true  
```

items.name: set
items.signature: function set(name: str, value: str): boolean
items.doc:
Sets or replaces an environment variable in the current process.  
  
The mutation is process-local: later calls to `Env::get` in this process  
observe the new value, and child processes spawned after the call inherit  
it. Already-running processes are not affected.  
  
Returns `true` when the host `setenv` call succeeds and `false` otherwise.  
Passing an empty `value` creates a present variable whose value is empty; it  
does not unset the variable.  
  
# Arguments  
  
- `name`: environment variable name to create or replace.  
- `value`: new variable value.  
  
# Returns  
  
`true` if `setenv(name, value, 1)` succeeds, otherwise `false`.  
  
# Failure Modes  
  
Host `setenv` can fail when `name` is invalid for the C runtime, for  
example an empty name or a name containing `=`. This API does not currently  
expose `errno`; it reports failure as `false`.  
  
# Example  
  
```ignis  
import Env from "std::env";  
  
if (Env::set("IGNIS_LOG", "trace")) {  
  let enabled: boolean = Env::has("IGNIS_LOG");  
}  
```

items.name: unset
items.doc:
Removes an environment variable from the current process.  
  
After a successful unset, `Env::has(name)` is `false` and `Env::get(name)`  
returns `Option::NONE`. Child processes created after the call do not  
inherit the removed variable from this process environment.  
  
# Arguments  
  
- `name`: environment variable name to remove.  
  
# Returns  
  
`true` if `unsetenv(name)` succeeds, otherwise `false`.  
  
# Failure Modes  
  
Host `unsetenv` can fail for invalid names. Removing a variable that is  
already absent is treated as a successful no-op on the supported POSIX  
hosts used by the std test suite.  
  
# Example  
  
```ignis  
import Env from "std::env";  
  
Env::set("IGNIS_TEMP", "1");  
Env::unset("IGNIS_TEMP");  
let missing: boolean = !Env::has("IGNIS_TEMP");  
```

items.name: var
items.doc:
Returns an owned environment value or an `EnvError` when it is missing.  
  
This is the `Result`-oriented variant of `Env::get` for required  
configuration. Missing variables return `Result::ERROR(EnvError { name })`;  
present empty variables return `Result::OK(String::create(""))`.  
  
# Arguments  
  
- `name`: required environment variable name.  
  
# Returns  
  
- `Result::OK(value)` with an owned copy when present.  
- `Result::ERROR(EnvError { name })` when missing.  
  
# Difference From `get`  
  
`get` is best for optional configuration. `var` is best when the caller  
wants absence to participate in normal `Result` error propagation with `!`.  
  
# Example  
  
```ignis  
import Env from "std::env";  
  
match (Env::var("PATH")) {  
  Result::OK(path) -> {},  
  Result::ERROR(error) -> {},  
};  
```

items.name: FFI
items.doc:
Re-export namespace for FFI helper types.  
  
Importing `std::ffi` makes `FFI::CString` and `FFI::NulError` available  
without referencing the implementation submodule directly.

items.name: FFI
items.doc:
Foreign Function Interface helpers.  
  
Currently this namespace provides owned C-string construction for APIs that  
require NUL-terminated pointers without interior NUL bytes.

items.name: CString
items.doc:
Owned C-compatible NUL-terminated string.  
  
`CString` represents an owned string that is guaranteed to:  
- Have no interior NUL bytes  
- Be NUL-terminated  
- Be allocated with the Ignis runtime allocator  
  
Use `CString` when passing strings to C functions that expect  
`const char*` or `char*` arguments.  
  
# Memory Layout  
  
```text  
  CString { data: 0x1000, len: 5 }  
  
  Memory at 0x1000:  
  ┌───┬───┬───┬───┬───┬───┐  
  │ h │ e │ l │ l │ o │ 0 │  
  └───┴───┴───┴───┴───┴───┘  
    0   1   2   3   4   5  
                  len NUL terminator  
```  
  
# Invariants  
  
- `data` points to a buffer of `len + 1` bytes allocated with `Memory::alloc`  
- `data[0..len]` contains no NUL bytes (0x00)  
- `data[len]` is NUL (0x00)  
- `data` is owned: automatically freed in `drop`  
  
# Safety  
  
- `fromRawOwned()` only accepts pointers from `intoRaw()` or the same  
  runtime allocator (`Memory::alloc` / `Memory::free`). Passing pointers  
  from `malloc`, static storage, or any other allocator is undefined  
  behavior.  
- Do not call `asStr()` if `data == null` (empty CString from  
  `fromRawOwned(null)`); passing a null pointer to C functions that  
  expect a valid string is undefined behavior.

members.name: data
members.doc: Owned pointer to the buffer. `char*` in C semantics.

members.name: len
members.doc: Length in bytes excluding the NUL terminator.

members.name: fromRawOwned
members.doc:
Recovers ownership of a raw pointer previously obtained from `intoRaw()`.  
  
# Safety (hard rules)  
  
- `ptr` MUST have been returned by `intoRaw()` from a `CString`  
- OR `ptr` MUST have been allocated with the same allocator as `Memory::alloc`  
- `ptr` MUST be NUL-terminated with no interior NULs  
- Passing pointers from `malloc`, static storage, or other allocators is UB  
  
# Arguments  
  
* `ptr` - Owned pointer to the buffer, or `null` for an empty `CString`  
  
# Returns  
  
A `CString` taking ownership of the buffer. If `ptr == null`, returns  
an empty `CString` with `data == null` and `len == 0`.  
  
# Warning  
  
Do not call `asStr()` on a `CString` created with `fromRawOwned(null)`.

members.name: new
members.doc:
Creates a `CString` from a `str` literal (`const char*`).  
  
Copies the bytes into a new owned buffer. Returns an error if the  
string contains interior NUL bytes.  
  
# Arguments  
  
* `s` - NUL-terminated string literal (caller guarantees NUL termination)  
  
# Returns  
  
- `Result::OK(CString)` if no interior NULs were found  
- `Result::ERROR(NulError)` with the position of the first NUL byte

members.name: ofString
members.doc:
Creates a `CString` from a `String` by reference.  
  
Gets the underlying `str` view from the `String` and scans for  
interior NUL bytes with `memchr`. If none are found, copies the  
bytes into a new owned buffer in a single `memcpy`.  
  
# Arguments  
  
* `s` - Reference to the source `String`  
  
# Returns  
  
- `Result::OK(CString)` if no interior NULs were found  
- `Result::ERROR(NulError)` with the position of the first NUL byte

members.name: asStr
members.doc:
Returns the contents as `const char*` for passing to C functions.  
  
The returned pointer is valid as long as the `CString` exists and  
is not modified.  
  
# Safety  
  
Do not call this method if `data == null` (empty `CString` created  
with `fromRawOwned(null)`). Passing a null pointer to C functions  
that expect a valid string is undefined behavior.  
  
# Returns  
  
Pointer to the NUL-terminated buffer (`const char*`).

members.name: drop
members.doc:
Releases the owned buffer.  
  
Called automatically when the `CString` goes out of scope via  
`@implements(Drop)`. Can also be called manually to release  
memory early.  
  
# Safety  
  
After calling `drop()`, the `CString` is empty and `asStr()` must  
not be called.

members.name: intoRaw
members.doc:
Extracts the owned buffer pointer and leaves the `CString` empty.  
  
After calling this method, the caller is responsible for freeing the  
buffer with `Memory::free`. The `CString` is left in an empty state.  
  
# Returns  
  
Owned pointer to the buffer (`char*`).

items.name: RawStat
items.doc:
Host `struct stat`, laid out field for field.  
  
`stat(2)` fills a caller-provided struct whose layout is fixed by the  
target's kernel ABI, not by POSIX. On x86_64 Linux that layout is the  
kernel's `stat` for the architecture, including the padding word after  
`st_gid`, the three `timespec` pairs, and three reserved words at the end.  
Every member is listed, including the ones this module never reads, so the  
record's size and every offset match the struct the kernel writes.  
  
The record exists only for the target its layout was checked against, so a  
target without one fails to compile rather than reading the wrong bytes.  
Adding a target means adding its layout under its own `@configFlag`.

items.name: RequestParser
items.doc:
A sans-IO HTTP/1.1 request parser for one connection.  
  
`feed` copies bytes in; `next` reports `HEAD`, then zero or more  
`BODY_CHUNK`, then `DONE` for each request, and `NEED_MORE` whenever  
it has to wait. Bytes after a request belong to the next one, so  
keep-alive and pipelined requests need nothing special.

Decides how the body is delimited (RFC 9112 section 6.3).  
  
`Transfer-Encoding` together with `Content-Length` is rejected as request  
smuggling. The only transfer coding accepted is a lone `chunked`. Every  
`Content-Length` element, across repeated fields and comma lists, has to  
be a valid count and all of them have to agree.

items.doc:
Parses `chunk-size [ BWS ";" chunk-ext ]` from `buffer[start..end]`.  
Extensions are skipped without interpretation. A size larger than  
`allowed` is `BODY_TOO_LARGE`, reported before the size can overflow.

`buffer[start..end]`. `end` is the start of the blank line that closes it.

items.doc:
What a server calls for every complete request. The handler fills  
`response`; the driver writes it once `handle` returns.  
  
`Server::run` shares one handler among all its threads, so `handle`  
takes `&self` and may run on several threads at once. State a handler  
changes has to sit behind a `Mutex` or an atomic.

The header fields.

The request method.

items.name: Response
items.doc:
The answer a handler builds: status 200, no header fields and an  
empty body until the handler changes them.  
  
The driver adds `Content-Length` and, when it closes the connection,  
`Connection: close`. A `Content-Length` or `Transfer-Encoding` the  
handler sets is dropped. A status outside 100 to 999, or a header name  
or value that could split the response (CR, LF), makes the driver send  
a 500 without a body instead.

members.doc: Replaces every header field named `name` with one holding `value`.

items.name: Server
items.doc: A blocking HTTP/1.1 server bound to an address.

members.name: bind
members.signature: static bind(address: &SocketAddress, config: ServerConfig): Result<Server, IoError>
members.doc:
Binds a listening socket to `address`. Port 0 picks a free port;  
`localAddress` reports which.

members.name: localAddress
members.doc: The address the server is bound to.

members.name: run
members.doc:
Serves connections with `handler` on `config.threads` threads.  
  
Each thread runs `acceptConnections`: it accepts a connection,  
serves it with `serveConnection` and accepts the next one. An error on a connection ends only that  
connection. A thread stops when `accept` fails, and `run` returns  
once every thread stopped, with the first thread's error. There is  
no way to stop a running server yet, so in practice `run` blocks for  
as long as the process lives.  
  
The workers carry the failing errno as an `i32` rather than an  
`IoError`: the error's message borrows a C-managed buffer, which makes  
`IoError` a view, and a view cannot cross a thread boundary. The  
errno is mapped back to an `IoError` on the calling thread.

items.name: ServerConfig
items.doc: How a server runs and what it accepts from a connection.

members.name: threads
members.doc:
Threads accepting and serving connections. Each serves one  
connection at a time. Default 8; 0 counts as 1.

members.name: limits
members.doc: The parser limits for every request.

members.name: idleTimeout
members.doc:
How long a read may wait for the client, between requests or within  
one. When it expires the connection is closed without a response.  
Default 30 seconds.

members.name: maxRequestsPerConnection
members.doc:
Requests served on one connection before the server closes it; 0  
means no limit. Default 0.

members.name: new
members.doc: The default configuration.

items.name: acceptConnections
items.doc:
Accepts connections on `listener` and serves each in turn with  
`handler` on the calling thread, until `accept` reports that the  
listener itself is unusable; returns that error's raw errno, and `0`  
is never returned on that path.  
  
Every thread of `Server::run` runs this loop. Calling it directly on  
threads of your own gives each thread its own handler, for state that  
is not `Send` or `Sync` (`std::web` builds one router per thread this  
way); the listener is shared, for example through an `Arc`.  
  
Any other `accept` failure concerns one connection or a passing  
shortage (a client that reset before it was accepted, no descriptors  
left), so the loop keeps going; after a shortage it waits briefly  
instead of spinning. An error on one connection only ends that  
connection.  
  
The errno is returned instead of an `IoError` so the value can cross a  
thread boundary: the error's message borrows a C-managed buffer, which  
makes `IoError` a view. Map it back with `Io::IoError::fromErrno`.

items.name: serveConnection
items.signature: function serveConnection<H>(stream: &mut TcpStream, handler: &H, config: &ServerConfig): Result<void, IoError>
items.doc:
Serves HTTP/1.1 requests on `stream` until the connection ends.  
  
Reads with `config.idleTimeout`, feeds the parser and calls `handler`  
for every complete request, then writes its response. The connection  
stays open for the next request unless the request does not keep it  
alive (see `RequestHead.keepAlive`), the response carries  
`Connection: close`, or `config.maxRequestsPerConnection` is reached.  
  
A malformed request gets a response with the parser's status and  
`Connection: close`, and ends the connection. A client that closes,  
or sends nothing for `config.idleTimeout`, ends it without a response.  
The body is passed to the handler only once complete, so  
`Expect: 100-continue` is not answered: the client sends the body  
after its own wait. A `HEAD` request gets the head the handler's  
response would have, without the body.  
  
Returns `OK` when the connection ended in one of these ways, and the  
error when reading or writing the socket failed.

items.name: isUtf8
items.doc:
Whether `bytes` is well-formed UTF-8: no truncated or overlong sequence,  
no surrogate and nothing above U+10FFFF.

items.name: lingerClose
items.doc:
Ends a connection the server decided to close: shuts the writing side,  
then reads and discards what the client still sends for a short while, so  
unread input does not make the close reset the connection before the  
client has read the response.

items.name: responseHead
items.doc:
The head the driver writes for `response`: its status and header fields,  
without any `Content-Length` or `Transfer-Encoding` the handler set, since  
the driver frames the body itself, and with `Connection: close` when the  
connection closes after it.

items.name: serializeResponse
items.signature: function serializeResponse(response: &Response, isHead: boolean, close: boolean): Vector<u8>
items.doc:
Serializes the answer to one request. A head that cannot be written  
becomes a 500 without a body.

items.name: Io
items.doc:
Standard I/O namespace.  
  
`println` and `eprintln` have overloads for both `String` and `str`.  
  
`String` overloads consume/move the value. `str` overloads forward the  
C string directly.

items.name: eprint
eprintln
items.doc:
Prints `message` to stderr followed by a newline (`\n`).  
  
Use this for error messages, warnings, and diagnostic output  
that should not mix with normal stdout.  
  
# Arguments  
  
* `message` - The String to print (consumed/moved).  
  
# Example  
  
```ignis  
import Io from "std::io";  
  
Io::eprintln(String::create("error: file not found"));  
Io::eprintln("error from str");  
```
